arXiv:2410.00127v3 [math.CO] 30 Jun 2026

Rook matroids and log-concavity of PP-Eulerian polynomials

Per Alexandersson Address: Department of Mathematics, Stockholm University, SE-106 91 Stockholm, Sweden Email address: per.w.alexandersson@gmail.com and Aryaman Jal Address: Fakultät für Mathematik, Ruhr-Universität Bochum, 44801 Bochum, Germany Email address: aryaman.jal@rub.de
Abstract.

We define and study rook matroids, the bases of which correspond to non-nesting rook placements on a skew Ferrers board. We show that rook matroids are a subclass of both transversal matroids and positroids; they also bear a subtle relationship to lattice path matroids that centers around not having the quaternary matroid Q6Q_{6} as a minor. The enumerative and distributional properties of non-nesting rook placements stand in contrast to those of usual rook placements: the non-nesting rook polynomial is not real-rooted in general, and is instead ultra-log-concave. We leverage this property together with a correspondence between rook placements and linear extensions of a poset to show that if PP is a naturally labeled width two poset, then the PP-Eulerian polynomial WPW_{P} is ultra-log-concave. This takes an important step towards resolving a log-concavity conjecture of Brenti (1989) and completes the story of the Neggers–Stanley conjecture for naturally labeled width two posets.

Key words and phrases:
Matroid, transversal matroid, rook placement, lattice path, log-concavity, real-rootedness, partially ordered set, Lorentzian polynomials, Neggers–Stanley conjecture

1. Introduction

1.1. Overview

Matroids can be defined from a wide variety of combinatorial objects. For example, the spanning trees of a graph, transversals of a set system, and dimers of a plabic graph respectively give rise to graphic matroids, transversal matroids [EF65], and positroids [Pos06]. A particularly well-behaved subclass of both transversal matroids and positroids is formed by the lattice path matroids introduced by Bonin, de Mier, and Noy [BdMN03, BdM06]. The bases of a lattice path matroid 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} can be viewed as lattice paths contained within some skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu. These matroids are known to have rich combinatorics; see [BdMN03] for a connection to the so-called tennis ball problem. They also play an important role in the algebro-combinatorial study of valuative invariants of matroids [Ham17, Fer23, FS24].

In this paper, we introduce a new class of matroids, also parametrized by skew shapes, that shares many of the properties of lattice path matroids while being distinct from them. Given a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu, the bases of the rook matroid ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} correspond to non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu, i.e., rook placements such that no rook lies South-East of another. We prove that, analogous to lattice path matroids, rook matroids are transversal and positroids; they are also closed under taking duals and direct sums. Moreover, the lattice path matroid and rook matroid on the same skew shape have the same Tutte polynomial, and hence the same number of bases, independent sets, spanning sets, and other invariants obtained as numerical specializations of the Tutte polynomial. However, despite sharing many of the same invariants, the two matroids are not isomorphic in general; one contribution of this work is to identify precisely when an isomorphism exists and construct one explicitly. This hinges on whether or not λ/μ\lambda/\mu contains 332/1332/1 as a subshape; equivalently, whether or not the rook matroid contains the quaternary matroid Q6Q_{6} as a minor.

Changing direction, we then apply the matroidal structure of non-nesting rook placements to prove that for a naturally labeled poset of width two, the corresponding PP-Eulerian polynomial is ultra-log-concave, thereby making progress on a conjecture of Brenti [Bre89]. The context of this result is the Neggers–Stanley conjecture [Neg78, Sta89], which asserted that WP,ωW_{P,\omega}, the (P,ω)(P,\omega)-Eulerian polynomial of a labeled poset, is real-rooted. This was disproved by Brändén [Brä04] and Stembridge [Ste07] in the early 2000s, the latter of whom provided a naturally labeled counterexample of width two. Despite these developments, the question of what weaker distributional property — for example, log-concavity or unimodality — holds for WP,ωW_{P,\omega} has remained open, with some progress in the graded, naturally labeled case [RW05, Brä08]. By deducing the strongest possible distributional property for WPW_{P}, our results thus complete the picture of the Neggers–Stanley conjecture in the naturally labeled, width two case. We do so by exhibiting a bijection between rook placements and linear extensions to show that a certain multivariate analog of WPW_{P} is a Lorentzian polynomial in the sense of Brändén and Huh [BH20].

1.2. Outline and main results

In Section 2, we gather background material on rook placements, distributional properties of combinatorial sequences, and matroid theory. The following is a summary of our main contributions together with the organization of the rest of the paper:

  1. (1)

    In Section 3, we define the rook matroid ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} (Theorem 3.3) via the transversal description and study some of its properties. We show that rook matroids are positroids (Theorem 3.26), give a precise criterion on λ/μ\lambda/\mu for when the rook matroid is isomorphic to the corresponding lattice path matroid 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} (Theorem 3.22), and prove that ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} and 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} are nevertheless Tutte-equivalent in all cases (Theorem 3.29).

  2. (2)

    In Section 4, we show that the generating polynomial Mλ/μ​(t)M_{\lambda/\mu}(t) of the size of non-nesting rook placements on a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is ultra-log-concave and not real-rooted in general. We give the first example of a lattice path matroid that does not have the half-plane property (Theorem 4.3), answering a question that was raised in [COSW04] regarding transversal matroids with the half-plane property.

  3. (3)

    In Section 5, we derive a bijective correspondence between skew shapes λ/μ\lambda/\mu and width two posets PP that maps non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu to linear extensions (Theorem 5.4) of PP. Consequently, the PP-Eulerian polynomial can be expressed as Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu}, settling the ultra-log-concavity consequence of the Neggers–Stanley conjecture for this class of posets (Corollary 5.8). We end by describing precisely when Mλ/μ​(t)M_{\lambda/\mu}(t) is gamma-positive.

2. Preliminaries

In this section, we define the basic combinatorial objects that will be the focus of our interest: non-nesting rook placements on boards and their generating polynomials. We will also recall the necessary background on matroids and notions from the geometry of polynomials that will be used in later sections.

2.1. Boards, skew shapes and rook placements

We use [n][n] to mean the set {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\dotsc,n\} and [m,n][m,n] to mean the discrete interval {m,m+1,…,n}\{m,m+1,\dotsc,n\}. The set of size-kk subsets of [n][n] is denoted by ([n]k)\binom{[n]}{k}.

A board BB with rr rows and cc columns is a subset of the rectangular grid [r]×[r+1,r+c][r]\times[r+1,r+c]. We label the rows with elements from [r][r] and the columns with elements from [r+1,r+c][r+1,r+c] respectively, as in Example 2.1. The row labeling is done from the top to bottom and the column labeling is done from left to right. We refer to cells (i,j)(i,j) of BB with respect to this labeling unless otherwise specified. Given a board BB with rr rows and cc columns, the bipartite graph corresponding to BB is the graph ΓB=([1,r]⊔[r+1,r+c],E)\Gamma_{B}=([1,r]\sqcup[r+1,r+c],E) where i∈[1,r]i\in[1,r] is connected to j∈[r+1,r+c]j\in[r+1,r+c] if (i,j)∈B(i,j)\in B. For most of what follows, we restrict ourselves to special classes of boards coming from integer partitions.

An integer partition λ=(λ1,…,λn)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}) is any non-increasing tuple of positive integers. Following the English convention, the Ferrers diagram of λ\lambda is a left-justified, weakly decreasing array of boxes. Two special partitions correspond to Ferrers diagrams in the shape of a staircase and rectangle, respectively. For the former, δn\delta_{n} denotes the partition (n,n−1,…,1)(n,n-1,\ldots,1) and for the latter, (a)b(a)^{b} denotes the partition consisting of bb parts each of size aa.

Given two integer partitions λ⊇μ\lambda\supseteq\mu of length at most rr, we let the skew Ferrers board associated with λ/μ\lambda/\mu be the board with cells

{(i,r+j):1≤i≤r​ and ​μi<j≤λi}.\left\{(i,r+j):1\leq i\leq r\text{ and }\mu_{i}<j\leq\lambda_{i}\right\}.

When μ\mu is the empty partition, we treat μ\mu as the all-zeros vector. In what follows, we also refer to a skew Ferrers board as a skew shape. We call a skew shape non-degenerate if for all ii, λi>μi\lambda_{i}>\mu_{i} and every column of the bounding rectangle contains at least one cell of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. A subshape of a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is the skew shape obtained by deleting rows or columns of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. The size of a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is the number of boxes in its diagram and is denoted |λ/μ||\lambda/\mu|. An outer corner of λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a cell (i,j)∉λ/μ(i,j)\notin\lambda/\mu such that (i,j−1),(i−1,j)∈λ/μ(i,j-1),(i-1,j)\in\lambda/\mu. An inner corner of λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a cell (i,j)∉λ/μ(i,j)\notin\lambda/\mu such that (i+1,j),(i,j+1)∈λ/μ(i+1,j),(i,j+1)\in\lambda/\mu.

By a non-attacking placement of rooks on a board, we mean a configuration of rooks where no two rooks can take each other in the sense of chess. More formally, a non-attacking rook placement ρ\rho on a board BB is a subset of BB, no two cells of which share a row or column index. Two rooks in a non-attacking rook placement form a nesting if one rook lies South-East of another. Hereafter, a non-nesting rook placement (or just rook placement, when it is clear that the setting is a non-nesting one) on a board BB is a non-attacking rook placement such that no pair of rooks forms a nesting. It is straightforward to see that a non-attacking rook placement on BB corresponds to a matching of the graph ΓB\Gamma_{B}.

We will frequently move between the settings of non-nesting rook placements and lattice paths in a skew shape. By such a lattice path, we mean a path starting from the Southwest corner of λ/μ\lambda/\mu and terminating at the Northeast corner of λ/μ\lambda/\mu that consists only of North and East steps. Examples can be found in Section 3.2.

We denote the set of non-nesting rook placements on a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu by NNλ/μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu}} and define the generating polynomial of its kk-subsets as follows.

Definition 2.2.

Given a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu with rr rows, the non-nesting rook polynomial of λ/μ\lambda/\mu is defined by

Mλ/μ​(t)=∑k=0rrk​(λ/μ)​tk,M_{\lambda/\mu}(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{r}r_{k}(\lambda/\mu)t^{k},

where rk​(λ/μ)r_{k}(\lambda/\mu) is the number of non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu of size kk.

Note that the degree of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} equals the length of the longest Northeast to Southwest diagonal that fits inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu, which is not necessarily equal to rr.

Mλa,b​(t)=∑k=0min⁡(a,b)(ak)​(bk)​tk.M_{\lambda_{a,b}}(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\min(a,b)}\binom{a}{k}\binom{b}{k}t^{k}.

This can be seen directly: choose a set {j1<…<jk}\{j_{1}<\ldots<j_{k}\} of columns in (ak)\binom{a}{k} ways and choose a set of rows {i1>…>ik}\{i_{1}>\ldots>i_{k}\} independently in (bk)\binom{b}{k} ways. Form the rook placement with cells {(iℓ,jℓ):ℓ=1,…k}\{(i_{\ell},j_{\ell}):\ell=1,\ldots k\}; by virtue of the ordering, this must be non-nesting.

By specializing a=b=na=b=n, we obtain the type B Narayana polynomial:

W⁡(t)=∑k=0n(nk)2​tk.W(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^{2}t^{k}.
Example 2.4 (Narayana polynomials).

The non-nesting rook polynomial for the staircase Ferrers board λ=δn=(n,n−1,n−2,…,2,1)\lambda=\delta_{n}=(n,n-1,n-2,\dotsc,2,1) is

Mδn​(t)=t−1​Nn+1​(t),M_{\delta_{n}}(t)=t^{-1}N_{n+1}(t),

where Nn​(t)=∑k=1n1n​(nk)​(nk−1)​tkN_{n}(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{n}\binom{n}{k}\binom{n}{k-1}t^{k} denotes the nthn^{\textnormal{th}} Narayana polynomial. This connection with lattice paths is addressed in greater generality in Section 3.2.

Distributional properties and multivariate generalizations of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu}, together with its realizability as a PP-Eulerian polynomial of a poset, will be studied in later sections.

2.2. Matroids

We use the following axiomatization of matroids in terms of its bases; for any undefined terms hereafter we refer the reader to [Oxl11].

Definition 2.5.

A matroid MM is a pair (E,ℬ)(E,\mathcal{B}) where EE is a finite set and ℬ\mathcal{B} is a collection of subsets of EE, called bases, satisfying the following two properties:

  1. (1)

    ℬ≠∅\mathcal{B}\neq\emptyset.

  2. (2)

    For each distinct pair B1,B2B_{1},B_{2} in ℬ\mathcal{B} and element a∈B1∖B2a\in B_{1}\setminus B_{2}, there exists b∈B2∖B1b\in B_{2}\setminus B_{1} such that (B1∖{a})∪{b}∈ℬ(B_{1}\setminus\{a\})\cup\{b\}\in\mathcal{B}.

The second property above is referred to as the basis-exchange axiom for matroids. Numerous other axiomatizations of matroids exist; some can be found in [Oxl11, Chapter 1]. One such axiomatization can be made in terms of independent sets. A set I⊂EI\subset E is an independent set of a matroid M=(E,ℬ)M=(E,\mathcal{B}) if I⊆BI\subseteq B, for some B∈ℬB\in\mathcal{B}.

An important example of matroids is the uniform matroid Uk,nU_{k,n}, defined as the matroid with ground set [n][n] and bases given by all kk-subsets of [n][n]. We recount more terminology associated to matroids.

  1. (1)

    A loop of a matroid MM is an element of the ground set not contained in any basis of MM. A coloop is an element of the ground set that is contained in every basis of MM.

  2. (2)

    Given a matroid M=(E,ℬ)M=(E,\mathcal{B}) and an element e∈Ee\in E, the deletion and contraction of MM by ee are the matroids with ground set E∖eE\setminus e that are respectively denoted by M∖eM\setminus e and M/eM/e and the bases of which are respectively given by:

    ℬ⁡(M∖e)\displaystyle\mathcal{B}(M\setminus e) ={{B∈ℬ:e∉B}if e is not a coloop of M{B∖e:B∈ℬ}if e is a coloop of M\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\{B\in\mathcal{B}:e\notin B\}\quad&\text{if $e$ is not a coloop of $M$}\\ \{B\setminus e:B\in\mathcal{B}\}\quad&\text{if $e$ is a coloop of $M$}\end{cases}
    ℬ⁡(M/e)\displaystyle\mathcal{B}(M/e) ={{B∖e:B∈ℬ,e∈B}if e is not a loop of Mℬ⁡(M∖e)if e is a loop of M\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\{B\setminus e:B\in\mathcal{B},e\in B\}\quad&\text{if $e$ is not a loop of $M$}\\ \mathcal{B}(M\setminus e)\quad&\text{if $e$ is a loop of $M$}\end{cases}

    A matroid obtained from MM by a sequence of deletions and contractions is called a minor of MM. A class 𝒞\mathcal{C} of matroids is minor-closed if given a matroid M∈𝒞M\in\mathcal{C}, every minor of MM is also in 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

  3. (3)

    The dual of a matroid M=(E,ℬ)M=(E,\mathcal{B}) is the matroid M∗M^{*} on the ground set EE and bases ℬ⁡(M∗)={E∖B:B∈ℬ}\mathcal{B}(M^{*})=\{E\setminus B:B\in\mathcal{B}\}.

Transversals of set systems give rise to an important class of matroids. Given a set system 𝒩=(N1,…,Nr)\mathcal{N}=(N_{1},\ldots,N_{r}) of not necessarily distinct subsets NiN_{i} of some ground set EE, a transversal XX of 𝒩\mathcal{N} is a subset of EE consisting of rr distinct elements, one from each set in 𝒩\mathcal{N}: that is, X={ai:i=1,…,r}X=\{a_{i}:i=1,\ldots,r\} such that ai∈Nia_{i}\in N_{i} for i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r. A partial transversal of 𝒩\mathcal{N} is a transversal for some subsystem ℳ=(Ni)i∈J\mathcal{M}=(N_{i})_{i\in J} indexed by a subset J⊂[r]J\subset[r]. The following theorem due to Edmonds and Fulkerson laid the foundation for the theory of transversal matroids:

Theorem 2.6.

[EF65] The partial transversals of 𝒩\mathcal{N} are the independent sets of a matroid on EE.

Matroids that arise in this way are called transversal matroids and 𝒩=(N1,…,Nr)\mathcal{N}=(N_{1},\ldots,N_{r}) is called a presentation of the matroid. The bases of a transversal matroid are given by the maximal partial transversals of 𝒩\mathcal{N}. When 𝒩\mathcal{N} admits a transversal, the maximal partial transversals are precisely the transversals of 𝒩\mathcal{N}.

2.3. Real-rootedness, log-concavity and unimodality

In this subsection, we recall some basic notions in the geometry of polynomials.

Given a sequence of non-negative integers (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n}, it is convenient to work instead with its generating polynomial A⁡(t)=∑k=0nak​tkA(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{k}t^{k}. The following notions, listed in descending order of strength, encode distributional properties of the sequence:

  1. (1)

    The generating polynomial A⁡(t)A(t) is real-rooted if AA has only real roots as univariate polynomial. Note that by the non-negativity of the aka_{k}, the roots of AA will necessarily be non-positive.

  2. (2)

    The sequence (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n} is ultra-log-concave if

    (ak(nk))2≥ak−1(nk−1)⋅ak+1(nk+1)for all 1≤k≤n−1.\left(\dfrac{a_{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\right)^{2}\geq\dfrac{a_{k-1}}{\binom{n}{k-1}}\cdot\dfrac{a_{k+1}}{\binom{n}{k+1}}\quad\text{for all $1\leq k\leq n-1$.}
  3. (3)

    The sequence (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n} is log-concave if

    ak2≥ak−1⋅ak+1for all 1≤k≤n−1.a_{k}^{2}\geq a_{k-1}\cdot a_{k+1}\quad\text{for all $1\leq k\leq n-1$.}
  4. (4)

    The sequence (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n} is unimodal if there exists some 0≤m≤n0\leq m\leq n such that:

    a0≤a1≤…≤am−1≤am≥am+1≥…≥an.a_{0}\leq a_{1}\leq\ldots\leq a_{m-1}\leq a_{m}\geq a_{m+1}\geq\ldots\geq a_{n}.

The sequence (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n} has no internal zeros if

ai​aj>0⟹ak>0for all 0≤i<j<k≤n.a_{i}a_{j}>0\implies a_{k}>0\quad\text{for all $0\leq i<j<k\leq n$}.

As mentioned above, the following implications hold: (1)⟹(2)⟹(3)⟹(4)(1)\implies(2)\implies(3)\implies(4). Here (3)(3) implies (4)(4) only if (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n} has no internal zeros. For a comprehensive and modern survey of these notions, and some of their multivariate counterparts that are addressed in later sections of this paper, see [Brä15].

3. The rook matroid

In this section, we show that there is a natural matroid structure underpinning the set of non-nesting rook placements on a skew Ferrers board. The associated class of matroids is a dual-closed subclass of both transversal matroids and positroids. However, it is not minor-closed and therein lies the subtlety in the relationship between rook matroids and lattice path matroids. The schematic in Figure 1 summarizes the various containment and characterization properties that rook matroids satisfy with respect to other known classes of matroids; we will prove these in Sections 3.2 and 3.3.

We begin by studying the structural properties of the rook matroid that arise from its transversal description.

3.1. Structural results

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape. Throughout we draw and refer to Young diagrams λ\lambda and μ\mu in terms of the English convention, that is as a left-justified array of boxes. With this convention in place, we index the rows of λ/μ\lambda/\mu by {1,2,…,r}\{1,2,\dotsc,r\} and the columns by {r+1,…,r+c}\{r+1,\dotsc,r+c\}. We set Eλ/μ=[r+c]E_{\lambda/\mu}=[r+c].

Given a non-nesting rook placement ρ\rho on λ/μ\lambda/\mu, we associate to it the set R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ)R(\rho)\cup C(\rho) where R⁡(ρ)R(\rho) is the set of row indices that are not occupied by ρ\rho and C⁡(ρ)C(\rho) is the set of column indices that are occupied by ρ.\rho. Note that for each non-nesting rook placement ρ\rho, we have that |R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ)|=r|R(\rho)\cup C(\rho)|=r, the number of rows of the shape. We gather these sets into a single collection:

ℛλ/μ≔{R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ):ρ∈NNλ/μ},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}}\coloneqq\{R(\rho)\cup C(\rho):\rho\in\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu}\},

where as before NNλ/μ\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu} is the set of non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. We use the following elementary fact about diagrams characterizing skew shapes.

Fact 3.1.

A board BB is a skew shape if and only if for every pair of cells (i,j),(k,ℓ)∈B(i,j),(k,\ell)\in B with i<ki<k and j<ℓj<\ell, we also have (k,j),(i,ℓ)∈B(k,j),(i,\ell)\in B.

Given a skew shape, we may define a set system as follows. For i∈[r]i\in[r], let AiA_{i} be the set of column indices occupied by row ii together with ii, that is,

Ai={j∈[r+1,r+c]:(i,j)∈λ/μ}∪{i}.A_{i}=\{j\in[r+1,r+c]:(i,j)\in\lambda/\mu\}\cup\{i\}.

Then 𝒜λ/μ≔(A1,…,Ar){\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{A}_{\lambda/\mu}}\coloneqq(A_{1},\dotsc,A_{r}) is a set system on Eλ/μE_{\lambda/\mu} which defines a transversal matroid.

Example 3.2.

Consider the skew shape λ/μ=77553/42\lambda/\mu=77553/42.

This skew shape has corresponding set system

A1\displaystyle A_{1} ={1,10,11,12}\displaystyle=\{1,10,11,12\} A2\displaystyle A_{2} ={2,8,9,10,11,12}\displaystyle=\{2,8,9,10,11,12\} A3\displaystyle A_{3} ={3,6,7,8,9,10}\displaystyle=\{3,6,7,8,9,10\}

The non-nesting rook placement shown on the right above can be represented by R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ)={3,4,6,10,11}R(\rho)\cup C(\rho)=\{3,4,6,10,11\} where 11∈A111\in A_{1}, 10∈A210\in A_{2}, 3∈A33\in A_{3}, 4∈A44\in A_{4}, 6∈A56\in A_{5}.

Theorem 3.3.

The set ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} is the collection of bases of the transversal matroid with set system 𝒜λ/μ\mathcal{A}_{\lambda/\mu}.

Proof.

Given ρ∈NNλ/μ\rho\in\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu}, it is clear that R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ)R(\rho)\cup C(\rho) is a transversal of 𝒜λ/μ\mathcal{A}_{\lambda/\mu}. Indeed, if ρ\rho has no rook in row ii, match ii to AiA_{i}; if ρ\rho has a rook in row ii at r+jr+j, match r+jr+j to AiA_{i}. Since ρ\rho is non-attacking, the chosen elements are distinct.

Conversely, suppose we are given a transversal TT of 𝒜λ/μ\mathcal{A}_{\lambda/\mu}. Let [r]∖T={i1<⋯<ik}[r]\setminus T=\{i_{1}<\cdots<i_{k}\} and T∩[r+1,r+c]={r+j1,⋯,r+jk}T\cap[r+1,r+c]=\{r+j_{1},\cdots,r+j_{k}\} where j1>⋯>jkj_{1}>\cdots>j_{k}. We claim that ρ={(iℓ,r+jℓ):ℓ=1,…,k}\rho=\{(i_{\ell},r+j_{\ell}):\ell=1,\ldots,k\} is a non-nesting rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. By the ordering on iℓ,jℓi_{\ell},j_{\ell}, the rook placement ρ\rho is non-nesting; it remains to show that ρ\rho lies on λ/μ\lambda/\mu, that is, μiℓ<jℓ≤λiℓ\mu_{i_{\ell}}<j_{\ell}\leq\lambda_{i_{\ell}} for ℓ=1,…,k\ell=1,\ldots,k. For the first inequality, suppose there exists s∈[k]s\in[k] such that js≤μisj_{s}\leq\mu_{i_{s}}. Then, for t≤st\leq s and a≥sa\geq s, we have μit≥μis≥js≥ja\mu_{i_{t}}\geq\mu_{i_{s}}\geq j_{s}\geq j_{a}. This implies that for indices t≤st\leq s and a≥sa\geq s column r+jar+j_{a} does not have a cell in row iti_{t}. Hence the k−s+1k-s+1 column elements r+js,r+js+1,…,r+jkr+j_{s},r+j_{s+1},\ldots,r+j_{k}, would have to be chosen from the k−sk-s sets Ais+1,…,AikA_{i_{s+1}},\ldots,A_{i_{k}}, which contradicts the fact that TT is a transversal.

For the second inequality, suppose to the contrary that there exists s∈[k]s\in[k] such that js>λisj_{s}>\lambda_{i_{s}}. Then, for t≥st\geq s and a≤sa\leq s, we have λit≤λis<js≤ja\lambda_{i_{t}}\leq\lambda_{i_{s}}<j_{s}\leq j_{a}. This implies that for indices tt and aa in the aforementioned ranges, column r+jar+j_{a} does not have a cell in row iti_{t}. Hence the ss columns r+j1,…,r+jsr+j_{1},\ldots,r+j_{s} would have to be chosen from the s−1s-1 sets Ai1,…,Ais−1A_{i_{1}},\ldots,A_{i_{s-1}}, which contradicts the fact that TT is a transversal. Thus, ρ\rho is a non-nesting rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu with R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ)=TR(\rho)\cup C(\rho)=T, which completes the proof. ∎

Identifying the resulting matroid by its set of bases, we call ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} the rook matroid on λ/μ\lambda/\mu; for any matroid MM, we say that MM is a rook matroid if it is isomorphic to a rook matroid of the form ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}. The uniform matroid Uk,nU_{k,n} corresponds to the rook matroid on the (n−k)×k(n-k)\times k rectangle. Later on, we will see how rook matroids interact with other well-studied classes of matroids, including lattice path matroids and positroids.

Empty rows and columns have the expected matroidal interpretation. A column jj of λ/μ\lambda/\mu is empty if and only if the corresponding column label belongs to no set AiA_{i}, and hence is a loop of Rλ/μR_{\lambda/\mu}. Similarly, row ii is empty, equivalently λi=μi\lambda_{i}=\mu_{i}, if and only if Ai={i}A_{i}=\{i\}, and hence the row label ii is a coloop. Thus deleting empty columns and rows from the skew shape amounts to removing loops and coloops from the corresponding rook matroid.

It is natural to ask if the skew shape assumption is necessary in the above theorem and the proposition below confirms that this is true.

Proposition 3.4.

Let BB be a board with rr rows and cc columns, and let

ℬ={R⁡(σ)∪C⁡(σ):σ∈NNB},\mathcal{B}=\{R(\sigma)\cup C(\sigma):\sigma\in\mathrm{NN}_{B}\},

where NNB\mathrm{NN_{B}} denotes the set of non-nesting rook placements on BB. If M=([r+c],ℬ)M=([r+c],\mathcal{B}) is a matroid with bases ℬ\mathcal{B}, then the board BB must be equal to some skew shape.

Proof.

We begin by noting that if ii is a row index, then the bases of M/iM/i correspond to the non-nesting rook placements on BB such that row ii is not occupied. Similarly, if jj is a column index, then the bases of M∖jM\setminus j correspond to the non-nesting rook placements on BB such that column jj is not occupied.

Now suppose BB is not a skew shape. Then, by Fact 3.1, there exists (i,j),(k,ℓ)∈B(i,j),(k,\ell)\in B with i<ki<k and j<ℓj<\ell such that at least one of (k,j)(k,j) or (i,ℓ)(i,\ell) do not lie in BB. Let M1=(M∖Y)/XM_{1}=(M\setminus Y)/X where X=[r]∖{i,k}X=[r]\setminus\{i,k\} and Y=[r+1,r+c]∖{j,ℓ}Y=[r+1,r+c]\setminus\{j,\ell\}. Let M2M_{2} be the matroid obtained by deleting all loops and coloops of M1M_{1}. Then, by the observation in the first paragraph of this proof, M2M_{2} is isomorphic to the matroid M3=([4],ℬ′)M_{3}=([4],\mathcal{B}^{\prime}) where

ℬ′={R⁡(σ)∪C⁡(σ):σ∈NNB′},\mathcal{B}^{\prime}=\{R(\sigma)\cup C(\sigma):\sigma\in\mathrm{NN}_{B^{\prime}}\},

and B′B^{\prime} is one of the three boards in Figure 2. In each case, {2,3},{1,4}∈ℬ′\{2,3\},\{1,4\}\in\mathcal{B}^{\prime} and 3∈{2,3}∖{1,4}3\in\{2,3\}\setminus\{1,4\} but neither of {1,2}\{1,2\} nor {2,4}\{2,4\} are valid non-nesting rook placements on any of these boards. ∎

More can be said about the transversal structure of the rook matroid. A fundamental transversal matroid is a matroid MM that has a basis BB (called a fundamental basis) such that each cyclic flat FF of MM is spanned by some subset of BB. An equivalent characterization identifies fundamental transversal matroids as those transversal matroids that have a presentation (A1,…,Ar)(A_{1},\ldots,A_{r}) such that for each i∈[r]i\in[r] there is some element in AiA_{i} that is in none of the other sets. This allows us to immediately note that rook matroids are fundamental transversal, as the distinguished element in each set of the presentation of ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} is simply the associated row label. The fundamental basis of the rook matroid then corresponds to the empty rook placement. See [BKdM11] for more about fundamental transversal matroids.

We now examine rook matroids through the structural properties of being closed under taking direct sums, duals, and minors. The first two properties hold while the third fails.

Lemma 3.5.

The class of rook matroids is closed under direct sums.

Proof.

A direct sum of rook matroids corresponds to the rook matroid on the direct sum of the corresponding skew shapes. That is, if λ1/μ1\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1} and λ2/μ2\lambda_{2}/\mu_{2} are two skew shapes, then the direct sum λ/μ≔(λ1/μ1)⊕(λ2/μ2)\lambda/\mu\coloneqq(\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1})\oplus(\lambda_{2}/\mu_{2}) is obtained by positioning the North-East corner of λ1/μ1\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1} to the immediate South-West of the South-West corner of λ2/μ2\lambda_{2}/\mu_{2}; see Figure 3. Then by the obvious isomorphism, ℛλ/μ≅ℛλ1/μ1⊕ℛλ2/μ2\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}\cong\mathcal{R}_{\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1}}\oplus\mathcal{R}_{\lambda_{2}/\mu_{2}}. ∎

The conjugate of a partition λ\lambda is the partition λ′\lambda^{\prime} obtained by taking the transpose of the Ferrers diagram of λ\lambda. Duals of rook matroids are simply rook matroids on conjugated skew shapes; the proof is straightforward and hence omitted.

Proposition 3.6.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape and let λ′/μ′\lambda^{\prime}/\mu^{\prime} denote its conjugate. Then the following isomorphism holds: ℛλ/μ∗≅ℛλ′/μ′\mathcal{R}^{*}_{\lambda/\mu}\cong\mathcal{R}_{\lambda^{\prime}/\mu^{\prime}}.

The following lemma shows that minors of rook matroids — in two cases — are straightforward to describe combinatorially. We make use of this lemma several times throughout the paper; its proof follows from the definitions of deletion and contraction.

Lemma 3.7.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape and ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} be the corresponding rook matroid. Suppose xx is a column index and yy is a row index of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Then

  • •

    The deletion ℛλ/μ∖x\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}\setminus x is isomorphic to the rook matroid obtained from the shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu with column xx removed;

  • •

    The contraction ℛλ/μ/y\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}/y is isomorphic to the rook matroid obtained from the shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu with row yy removed;

  • •

    The bases in the contraction ℛλ/μ/x\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}/x correspond to non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu where column xx is occupied by a rook;

  • •

    The bases in the deletion ℛλ/μ∖y\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}\setminus y correspond to non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu where row yy is occupied by a rook.

Rook matroids can even be shown to be closed under contraction, a fact that can be deduced using the theory developed in [Tof25]. We omit a proof of this to keep the current paper thematically coherent.

Despite the lemma and remark above, the property of being minor-closed fails for rook matroids: there are rook matroids whose deletion is not a rook matroid. The deeper reason for this failure is best understood in terms of the observation that minors of fundamental transversal matroids are rarely fundamental transversal. We thank Joe Bonin for suggesting an example that did not rely on exhaustive computer search, and for pointing out that the class of rook matroids on 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shapes is not minor-closed, as was claimed in an earlier version of this manuscript. The next example makes reference to lattice path matroids; see Section 3.2 for the definition.

Example 3.8.

Consider λ/μ=442/2\lambda/\mu=442/2, the skew shape shown on the left in Figure 4 and M=ℛλ/μM=\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}. The matroid M∖2M\setminus 2 can be seen to be isomorphic to the lattice path matroid 𝒫332/1\mathcal{P}_{332/1}, which is not a rook matroid. This is because the only possible candidate is ℛ332/1≅Q6\mathcal{R}_{332/1}\cong Q_{6} (proven below), which is a known excluded minor of lattice path matroids. Thus M∖2M\setminus 2 is not a rook matroid and rook matroids are not minor-closed.

Lemma 3.9.

The rook matroid ℛ332/1\mathcal{R}_{332/1} is isomorphic to the quaternary matroid Q6Q_{6}.

Proof.

By checking the two three-element circuits of each matroid, one sees that the map from {1,2,…,6}\{1,2,\ldots,6\} to {a,b,c,d,e,f}\{a,b,c,d,e,f\} defined as 1↦c,2↦f,3↦d,4↦a,5↦b,6↦e1\mapsto c,2\mapsto f,3\mapsto d,4\mapsto a,5\mapsto b,6\mapsto e is a matroid isomorphism between ℛ332/1\mathcal{R}_{332/1} and Q6Q_{6}. ∎

We note that Q6Q_{6} is an excluded minor for the class of lattice path matroids (see [Bon10, Theorem 3.1] where Q6Q_{6} appears in the list as A3A_{3}). For further properties of Q6Q_{6}, see [Oxl11, pg. 641]. We explore the link between 332/1332/1-avoiding shapes and lattice path matroids in greater depth in the next section.

3.2. Relation to lattice path matroids

In what follows we collect enumerative and matroidal results linking rook matroids to lattice path matroids, a well-studied family of transversal matroids that also arise from skew shapes. See [BdMN03, BdM06] for an introduction to lattice path matroids. The goal of this subsection is to identify precisely when a rook matroid and a lattice path matroid on the same skew shape are isomorphic.

Let m,r≥0m,r\geq 0 and U,LU,L be two lattice paths from (0,0)(0,0) to (m,r)(m,r) such that UU never goes below LL. (All lattice paths in this paper only consist of North and East steps.) Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be the skew shape defined by the region enclosed by UU and LL. Lattice paths can be uniquely identified by recording the indices of their North steps.

Denote by M⁡[U,L]M[U,L] the transversal matroid on [m+r][m+r] with presentation given by ℰ=(N1,…,Nr)\mathcal{E}=(N_{1},\ldots,N_{r}) where NjN_{j} are the North step sets defined by

Nj={i:i is the index of the jth North step of some lattice path P in λ/μ}.N_{j}=\{i:\text{$i$ is the index of the $j^{\textnormal{th}}$ North step of some lattice path $P$ in $\lambda/\mu$}\}.
Definition 3.10.

A lattice path matroid (LPM) is a matroid that is isomorphic to the matroid M⁡[U,L]M[U,L] for some lattice paths U,LU,L.

To emphasize the perspective of the matroid arising from a skew shape we will instead use the notation 𝒫λ/μ≔M⁡[U,L]{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}}\coloneqq M[U,L], where U,LU,L are respectively the upper and lower boundary paths of the diagram defined by the (possibly degenerate) skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu. After deleting empty rows and columns of λ/μ\lambda/\mu, the boundary paths UU and LL share no steps, so the associated lattice path matroid is loopless and coloopless. Note that when μ\mu is the empty partition, the lattice path matroid 𝒫λ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda} is called a Schubert matroid or generalized Catalan matroid [BdM06].

Our first result connecting rook matroids and lattice path matroids is a straightforward bijection that naturally leads to the question of when they are isomorphic.

For any skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu, it is easy to see that 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} and ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} have equal cardinality for the following reason. Define an inner valley of a lattice path in λ/μ\lambda/\mu to be a valley such that neither its East step nor its North step lies on the upper boundary of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Then, given any lattice path inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu, place a rook in each inner valley of the path. This defines a non-nesting rook placement, and this process is clearly reversible. We record this fact below for use later on in Section 5.

Proposition 3.11.

For any skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu, the map Tλ/μ:NNλ/μ→𝒫λ/μT_{\lambda/\mu}:\mathrm{NN}_{\lambda/\mu}\to\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} defined by fixing the inner valleys of the lattice path precisely at cells containing rooks is a bijection.

In particular, when λ\lambda is the staircase (n,n−1,…,1)(n,n-1,\dotsc,1), we obtain the bijection that yields the formula in Example 2.4. This connection facilitates an exact count of the number of non-nesting rook placements contained in λ/μ\lambda/\mu via the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot lemma; see [Kra15, Theorem 10.7.1] and [SP02, Eq. (6)], for example.

The bijection in Proposition 3.11 is not a matroid isomorphism in general. The goal for the remainder of this subsection is to characterize when ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} and 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} are isomorphic. As we noted in Section 3.1, the obstruction to this isomorphism comes from the skew shape 332/1332/1 where the lattice path matroid structure and rook matroid structure are not isomorphic. The more surprising fact is that this is the only obstruction for a rook matroid to be isomorphic to a lattice path matroid.

The next sequence of results develops the tools needed to define this matroid isomorphism using the combinatorics of skew shapes. The first notion involves dividing up the skew shape into rectangles.

Definition 3.12.

The rectangular decomposition of a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is the collection of rectangles partitioning the skew shape, each of which is formed by grouping together columns that share the same set of row indices.

An example of the rectangular decomposition of a skew shape is shown in Figure 7. We use the rectangular decomposition to give a characterization of 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shapes, that is the class of skew shapes not containing 332/1332/1 as a subshape. The following proposition gives three ways of describing this class.

Proposition 3.13.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a connected skew shape. Then the following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    The shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is 332/1332/1-avoiding.

  2. (ii)

    The shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu can be built from the skew shape consisting of a single cell by using a sequence of the following four operations: (I) duplicating the first row, (II) duplicating the last column, (III) adding a box to the first row, (IV) creating a new first row with a single box. These four operations are illustrated on the shape below:

  3. (iii)

    The rectangular decomposition of λ/μ\lambda/\mu satisfies the property that for any three consecutive rectangles R1,R2,R3R_{1},R_{2},R_{3}, we do not simultaneously have that

    1. (a)

      the top of R1R_{1} is strictly above the bottom of R3R_{3},

    2. (b)

      the top of R1R_{1} is strictly below the top of R2R_{2},

    3. (c)

      the bottom of R3R_{3} is strictly above the bottom of R2R_{2}.

Proof.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu occupy rr rows and cc columns. The equivalences are clear if either r≤2r\leq 2 or c≤2c\leq 2, so assume for the remainder of this proof that r,c≥3r,c\geq 3.

(i)⟹(i​i)(i)\implies(ii) Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape not satisfying (ii). We must show that the diagram must then contain 332/1332/1 as a subshape. We may assume that λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a minimal shape having this property. (Here we use minimal with respect to the size |λ/μ||\lambda/\mu| of the skew shape.)

By minimality, every proper subshape of λ/μ\lambda/\mu satisfies (ii), which implies that none of the inverses of the four operations in (ii) can be applied to λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Hence λ/μ\lambda/\mu satisfies the following properties:

  1. (1)

    The first two rows of λ/μ\lambda/\mu have different length.

  2. (2)

    The last two columns of λ/μ\lambda/\mu have different length.

  3. (3)

    The first and second row have their last cells in the same column.

  4. (4)

    The first row contains more than one box.

Properties (1) and (3) imply that λ/μ\lambda/\mu has an inner corner at the first row; let the corresponding column index of that corner be kk. Let the common column index in which the first two rows have their last cell be jj. The last two columns of the skew shape will then be j−1j-1 and jj. By property (2), columns j−1j-1 and jj have different length which implies that λ/μ\lambda/\mu has an outer corner in column jj; let the corresponding row index of that corner be s≥3s\geq 3, by the assumption on the number of rows and columns. Then λ/μ\lambda/\mu contains 332/1332/1 as a subshape since it has an inner corner at (1,k)(1,k), an outer corner at (s,j)(s,j) and columns kk to j−1j-1 — which by the assumption r,c≥3r,c\geq 3 are at least two in number — all have the same length.

(i​i)⟹(i​i​i)(ii)\implies(iii) Proceed by induction on |λ/μ||\lambda/\mu|; the base case holds vacuously. Assume the result holds for all skew shapes with size less than |λ/μ||\lambda/\mu|. Let the skew shape λ1/μ1\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1} be the shape before λ/μ\lambda/\mu to which one of the operations (I)-(IV) in point (ii) were applied and let 𝒟\mathcal{D} and 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} respectively be the collection of rectangles in the rectangular decompositions of λ/μ\lambda/\mu and λ1/μ1\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1}. Consider the operation that transformed λ1/μ1\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1} to λ/μ\lambda/\mu. If it was (I), then duplicating the top row maintains the relative heights of any three rectangles in 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} and hence (iii) holds for 𝒟\mathcal{D}. If it was (II), then only the width of the last rectangle in 𝒟\mathcal{D} changes while its heights stay the same, so (iii) holds for 𝒟\mathcal{D}. If the last operation was (III) and the number of rectangles in 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} increases, then the location of the bottom of the last rectangle in 𝒟\mathcal{D} strictly increases, which ensures that property (a) and (b) in point (iii) cannot hold simultaneously with R3R_{3} as this last rectangle. Finally, if the last operation is (IV), then in the non-trivial case, 𝒟\mathcal{D} has one more rectangle than 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} but this rectangle has the same bottom as the last rectangle in 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} so (c) does not hold.

(i​i​i)⟹(i)(iii)\implies(i) Suppose λ/μ\lambda/\mu contains 332/1332/1. We must show that there are three consecutive rectangles in the rectangular decomposition of λ/μ\lambda/\mu such that (a), (b), (c) hold for these.

Since λ/μ\lambda/\mu contains 332/1332/1 as a subshape, we can then find an inner corner (i1,j1)(i_{1},j_{1}) and an outer corner (i2,j2)(i_{2},j_{2}) of λ/μ\lambda/\mu such that the subshape of λ/μ\lambda/\mu consisting of rows i1i_{1} to i2i_{2} and columns j1+1j_{1}+1 to j2−1j_{2}-1 is a rectangle; call this R2R_{2}. Then if R1R_{1} is the rectangle consisting of column j1j_{1} and R3R_{3} is the rectangle consisting of column j2j_{2}, it is clear that rectangles R1,R2,R3R_{1},R_{2},R_{3} satisfy properties (a), (b), (c). See Figure 5 for an example of this on 332/1332/1 itself. This concludes the proof. ∎

We now introduce a tool that will give us a way to interpolate between rook placements and lattice paths. The idea is to represent a lattice path by a permutation the ithi^{\textnormal{th}} entry of which keeps track of which row or column index of the skew shape the ithi^{\textnormal{th}} step of the lattice path occupies, as counted from the bottom.

Definition 3.14 (Path permutation).

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape with rr rows and cc columns labeled in the usual way. The path permutation corresponding to LL is ψL=ψ1​…​ψr+c∈𝔖r+c\psi_{L}=\psi_{1}\ldots\psi_{r+c}\in\mathfrak{S}_{r+c}, where:

ψi={column index of the column occupied by step iif i is an East step,row index of the row occupied by step iif i is a North step.\psi_{i}=\begin{cases}\text{column index of the column occupied by step $i$}\quad&\text{if $i$ is an East step,}\\ \text{row index of the row occupied by step $i$}\quad&\text{if $i$ is a North step.}\end{cases}

We now define a special lattice path inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu that only exists when λ/μ\lambda/\mu is 332/1332/1-avoiding. The permutation corresponding to this path turns out to be precisely the bijection that will induce the matroid isomorphism between 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} and ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} shown ahead. In Section 5, the skew shape is given a different labeling; the path permutation with respect to this labeling plays a crucial role in the proof of the main result in that section.

Definition 3.16 (Spine path).

Suppose that λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shape contained in an r×cr\times c rectangle. Let R1,…,RkR_{1},\dotsc,R_{k} denote the rectangles in the rectangular decomposition of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. (Note that these rectangles satisfy item (iii) in Proposition 3.13.) We construct a lattice path LL of length r+cr+c as follows.

Start from the lower left hand corner of R1R_{1}.

  1. (i)

    If there is only one rectangle (k=1)(k=1) then let LL be the North–East boundary of R1R_{1}.

  2. (ii)

    If the bottom of R2R_{2} is not at the same level as the bottom of R1R_{1}, take North steps until the bottom of R2R_{2} is reached, and then East steps until the lower left corner of R2R_{2} is reached. Recursively construct the rest of LL from here based on the shape R2,R3,…,RkR_{2},R_{3},\dotsc,R_{k}.

  3. (iii)

    If k≥3k\geq 3, and if the bottom of R1R_{1} and R2R_{2} are the same, and the top of R1R_{1} is at the same level as the bottom of R3R_{3}, then take North steps until the top of R1R_{1} is reached, and then take East steps until the bottom left corner of R3R_{3} is reached. Recursively construct the rest of LL based on the shape R3,…,RkR_{3},\dotsc,R_{k}.

  4. (iv)

    In any other case, follow the North–East border of R1R_{1}. This ends somewhere on the left side of R2R_{2}, say at (p,q)(p,q). Now construct the rest of LL using the part of the shape which is North–East of (p,q)(p,q).

    Observe that we apply this case if (a) k=2k=2, (b) the bottoms of R1R_{1}, R2R_{2} and R3R_{3} are the same, or (c) when the bottom of R3R_{3} is strictly above the top of R2R_{2}.

    (Observe that the case when the bottom of R3R_{3} is strictly below the top of R1R_{1} does not appear, since this would violate the 332/1332/1-avoiding property, see Proposition 3.13, so we have covered all cases.)

See Figure 6 for an illustration of the four cases.

The resulting lattice path is called the spine path of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. By definition, the spine path is always contained inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu.

Example 3.17.

The spine path is particularly easy to construct for Ferrers shapes, see the first shape in Figure 7.

Below, when we refer to a North-East segment of LL, we mean the word 𝙽𝙴\mathtt{NE} as a subword of LL when written as a sequence of 𝙽\mathtt{N}s and 𝙴\mathtt{E}s.

Lemma 3.18.

Suppose LL is the spine path of a 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu, and consider a corner of the spine path formed by a North-East segment of LL occurring in row pp and column qq of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Then the subshape {(i,j)∈λ/μ:i≥p,j≥q}\{(i,j)\in\lambda/\mu:i\geq p,j\geq q\} of λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a rectangle.

Similarly, if an East–North corner of LL occurs in column qq and row pp, then the subshape {(i,j)∈λ/μ:i≤p,j≤q}\{(i,j)\in\lambda/\mu:i\leq p,j\leq q\} of λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a rectangle.

Remark 3.19.

See Figure 7 for an example of this property. The idea behind this lemma is that no run of East steps of the spine path intersects the interior of more than one rectangle in the rectangular decomposition of the skew shape.

Proof.

We only prove the statement concerning the North-East segments of LL since the other case can be proved analogously. Let R1,…,RkR_{1},\dotsc,R_{k} be the rectangles in the rectangular decomposition of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. We note that each rectangle in the rectangular decomposition of a skew shape can contain at most one subshape induced by a North-East segment; this is because any run of East steps of the spine path intersects the interior of at most one rectangle in the skew shape. Let D1,…,DkD_{1},\ldots,D_{k} be these (possibly empty) Ferrers shapes. If there is indeed a 𝙽𝙴\mathtt{NE} segment of LL in RiR_{i}, we will call DiD_{i} non-empty.

We proceed by induction on kk. When k=1k=1, λ/μ\lambda/\mu is itself a rectangle and LL is, by construction, the North-East boundary of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Hence the subshape formed by the only North-East segment of LL is also a rectangle.

If k=2k=2 or 33, the result follows by a casewise inspection of the relative heights of the rectangles R1,R2,R3R_{1},R_{2},R_{3} and the construction of the spine path in Definition 3.16.

Suppose now k>3k>3 and the result holds for all skew shapes with at most k−1k-1 rectangles in the rectangular decomposition. Let LL be the spine path of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. By construction of LL, the restriction of LL to the rectangles R1,…,Rk−3R_{1},\ldots,R_{k-3} is the spine path L′L^{\prime} of the skew shape with rectangular decomposition R1,…,Rk−3R_{1},\ldots,R_{k-3}. Applying the induction hypothesis to this skew shape and L′L^{\prime}, we see that each of D1,…,Dk−3D_{1},\ldots,D_{k-3} is a rectangle.

It remains to consider DiD_{i} for i=k−2,k−1i=k-2,k-1 and kk. If Dk−2D_{k-2} is non-empty, one of two cases can occur: (a) LL crosses the interior of Rk−2R_{k-2}. This corresponds to case (ii) in the spine path construction and hence Dk−2D_{k-2} is clearly a rectangle; or else we have (b) LL does not cross the interior of Rk−2R_{k-2}, in which instance either case (iii) or (iv) from the spine path construction holds. In each of these cases, the rectangle(s) succeeding Rk−2R_{k-2} have the same bottom as Rk−2R_{k-2} so once again Dk−2D_{k-2} is a rectangle. If Dk−1D_{k-1} is non-empty, only cases (ii) and (iv a) of the spine path construction can occur; in both cases it is immediate that Dk−1D_{k-1} is a rectangle. Finally by construction of the spine path, LL travels along the North-East boundary of RkR_{k} and hence DkD_{k} equals RkR_{k} itself and is hence a rectangle. ∎

For brevity, let ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu} be the path permutation determined by the spine path of λ/μ\lambda/\mu whenever λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shape. This is called the spine bijection for short. We will show that if λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shape then its spine bijection induces a bijection from the bases of 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} to the bases of ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}. By an abuse of notation, we call the induced map between set systems ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu}. Note that the spine bijection sends the basis in 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} corresponding to the spine path to the empty non-nesting rook placement in ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}. Before proceeding with the proof, we first give an example.

Example 3.20.

Consider the case λ=321\lambda=321. The spine bijection ψλ\psi_{\lambda} (in 2-line notation) and the corresponding spine path are shown below.

We can see by inspection that ψλ\psi_{\lambda} induces a bijection from lattice paths in 𝒫321\mathcal{P}_{321} to non-nesting rook placements in ℛ321\mathcal{R}_{321}. We illustrate the induced bijection ψ321:𝒫321→ℛ321\psi_{321}:\mathcal{P}_{321}\to\mathcal{R}_{321} below by drawing the lattice paths together with the corresponding non-nesting rook placements. Each shape is labeled with the lattice path basis on the left and its corresponding non-nesting rook placement basis on the right.

      
      

A crucial ingredient in generalizing the idea above is the presence of a spine path, which we know can only be defined for 332/1332/1-avoiding shapes. The following theorem shows that a rook matroid and lattice path matroid on the same skew Ferrers shape are isomorphic if and only if 332/1332/1 does not occur as a subshape of λ/μ\lambda/\mu.

Before we prove this, we introduce a definition that allows one to move between lattice paths contained inside a skew shape.

Definition 3.21.

Two lattice paths LL and L′L^{\prime} are related by a flip if LL can be obtained from L′L^{\prime} by either (a) flipping an East-North segment of L′L^{\prime} to a North-East segment, or (b) flipping a North-East segment to an East-North segment.

We are now ready to state the main theorem of this subsection. Since empty rows correspond to coloops and empty columns correspond to loops in both ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} and 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}, it is enough to prove the theorem below for non-degenerate skew shapes; one extends it by matching these corresponding coloops and loops.

Note: A matroidal proof of the first statement in Theorem 3.22 was later obtained in [BdM26] using properties of the configuration of a transversal matroid.

Theorem 3.22.

The lattice path matroid 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} is isomorphic to the rook matroid ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} if and only if λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shape. In that case, an explicit isomorphism from 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} to ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} is given by ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu}.

Proof.

For the only if direction: suppose λ/μ\lambda/\mu contains 332/1332/1 as a subshape. Then ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} would contain Q6Q_{6} as a minor by Lemma 3.9 and Lemma 3.7. But Q6Q_{6} is an excluded minor (see [Bon10, Thm. 3.1]) for the class of lattice path matroids so ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} cannot be isomorphic to 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}.

For the if direction: let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shape on rr rows and cc columns. Since λ/μ\lambda/\mu avoids 332/1332/1, we can consider its spine path L0L_{0} and the associated spine bijection ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu}, which for the purpose of brevity we occasionally refer to as ψ\psi. Recall that we are identifying a lattice path by its set of North steps. We will be done by the following claim:

Claim: If LL is a lattice path contained inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu, then ψλ/μ​(L)\psi_{\lambda/\mu}(L) defines a non-nesting rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu.

Proof of claim: We proceed by induction on kk, the number of cells between LL and the spine path. For the k=0k=0 case, LL is the spine path itself, the North steps of which, by construction, correspond to the row indices of λ/μ\lambda/\mu which implies that ψλ/μ​(L0)\psi_{\lambda/\mu}(L_{0}) is the empty rook placement.

In the two-line notation of the spine path permutation, we partition the columns into blocks, formed by runs of steps in the same direction (North or East).

Now suppose k≥1k\geq 1 and consider any lattice path L+L^{+} contained inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu with kk cells between it and L0L_{0}. Then L+L^{+} can be obtained from some lattice path LL in λ/μ\lambda/\mu with k−1k-1 cells between LL and L0L_{0} via a flip between steps ii and i+1i+1. Here ii and i+1i+1 are consecutive steps of the lattice path LL such that exactly one of them is a North step. This means that L+=(L∖{i})∪{i+1}L^{+}=(L\setminus\{i\})\cup\{i+1\} or L+=(L∖{i+1})∪{i}L^{+}=(L\setminus\{i+1\})\cup\{i\}.

In the two-line notation of ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu}, circle the North steps of LL, as in Example 3.23. By the induction hypothesis, the values below the circled entries, ψ⁡(L)\psi(L), define a valid non-nesting rook placement ρL\rho_{L} on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. The last sentence of the paragraph above implies that the set ψ⁡(L+)\psi(L^{+}) is obtained from ψ⁡(L)\psi(L) by swapping out one of ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) or ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) for the other. At the level of the circled entries of the first line of ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu}, the flipping of a 𝙽𝙴\mathtt{NE} segment to an 𝙴𝙽\mathtt{EN} segment or vice versa corresponds to moving a circle (the index of a North step) either one position left or right.

We will show that the swapping of ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) and ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) corresponds to a movement of some rooks of ρL\rho_{L} that still defines a valid non-nesting rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Recall that we have partitioned the columns of the two-line array of the spine bijection ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu} into blocks. There are four cases to consider:

  • A.

    ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) and ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) are both column indices from the same block.

  • B.

    ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) and ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) are both row indices from the same block.

  • C.

    ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) and ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) are in different blocks, and the North step (exactly one of ii or i+1i+1) is mapped to a column index.

  • D.

    ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) and ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) are in different blocks, and the North step of LL is mapped to a row index.

By Lemma 3.18, any such flip occurs in a rectangular region determined by the spine path. Note that such a rectangular region is given by row and column indices in two adjacent blocks in the two-line notation of ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu}.

We will see that in every case this corresponds to moving the rooks of ρL\rho_{L} such that they still stay on λ/μ\lambda/\mu, since all operations are performed on some rectangle, as guaranteed by Lemma 3.18. We consider each of the cases above.

  • A.

    In this case we have two adjacent columns ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) and ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) where one is empty the other is occupied by a rook of ρL\rho_{L}. We can then move the rook horizontally to the adjacent column and obtain a new valid rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu.

  • B.

    In this case we have two adjacent rows ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) and ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) where one is empty the other is occupied by a rook. The rook is moved vertically to the adjacent row to obtain a new valid rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu.

  • C.

    In this case, either p=ψ⁡(i)p=\psi(i) and q=ψ⁡(i+1)q=\psi(i+1) are respectively an occupied row and an occupied column, or vice versa.

    In the first case, we need to make both row pp and column qq unoccupied without affecting the occupancy of the other rows or columns, or the non-nesting nature of the other rooks of ρL\rho_{L}. (In the two-line array, this corresponds to moving a circle one step to the left.).

    There are two configurations to consider. Either the cell (p,q)(p,q) is occupied by a rook or not. In the former configuration, simply delete the rook in (p,q)(p,q). This is shown in the figure on the left below.

    →\;\to         →\;\to

    In the second configuration, we form a “staircase” of cells (marked ∘\circ) based on the location of the existing rooks in the rectangle North-West to (p,q)(p,q), as seen in the figure above on the right. We then move the rooks of ρL\rho_{L} to the locations marked ∘\circ, once again obtaining a new valid non-nesting rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu, without affecting the occupancy of any other row or column of ρL\rho_{L}.

    In the second case, pp is a column index and qq is a row index. The same operations as above are performed with the figures rotated by 180∘180^{\circ}. (In the two-line array, this corresponds to moving a circle one step to the right.)

  • D.

    As in C, there are two cases. In the first case, column q=ψ⁡(i)q=\psi(i) and row p=ψ⁡(i+1)p=\psi(i+1) are both unoccupied and need to be made occupied; the second case, where qq is a row and pp is a column, is treated analogously. Again, two configurations may arise: one where the rectangle strictly South-West of (p,q)(p,q) contains a rook, and one where it does not. In the former, simply place a rook at (p,q)(p,q). In the latter, perform the simultaneous shifting of rooks as in Case C. This is illustrated below.

    →\;\to         →\;\to

Once again, the second configuration in this case corresponds to the same picture rotated 180∘180^{\circ}. The consideration of the four cases is thus complete.

This shows that ψλ/μ​(L+)\psi_{\lambda/\mu}(L^{+}) also defines a non-nesting rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu, which proves the claim. Thus ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu} maps bases of 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} to bases of ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}. By Proposition 3.11, ℬ⁡(𝒫λ/μ)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}) and ℬ⁡(ℛλ/μ)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}) have equal cardinalities, and hence ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu} is a matroid isomorphism, completing the proof. ∎

In a different direction, we can obtain lattice path matroids as deletions of large enough rook matroids.

Proposition 3.24.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape with rr rows and n−rn-r columns. Define partitions λ∗,μ∗\lambda^{*},\mu^{*} by λi∗=λi+r−i+1\lambda_{i}^{*}=\lambda_{i}+r-i+1 and μi∗=μi+r−i\mu_{i}^{*}=\mu_{i}+r-i for i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r. Then 𝒫λ/μ≅ℛλ∗/μ∗∖[r]\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}\cong\mathcal{R}_{\lambda^{\ast}/\mu^{\ast}}\setminus[r].

Proof.

Recall that the sets in the transversal presentation of ℛλ∗/μ∗\mathcal{R}_{\lambda^{*}/\mu^{*}} are

Ai={i}∪{r+j:μi+r−i<j≤λi+r−i+1}for i=1,…,r.A_{i}=\{i\}\cup\{r+j:\mu_{i}+r-i<j\leq\lambda_{i}+r-i+1\}\quad\text{for $i=1,\ldots,r$}.

By deleting the elements of [r][r] from ℛλ∗/μ∗\mathcal{R}_{\lambda^{*}/\mu^{*}}, we are left with a transversal matroid on [r+1,r+n][r+1,r+n] whose ithi^{\textnormal{th}} set is the interval equal to the second set in the equation above. By applying the shift j↦j−rj\mapsto j-r, and reindexing with s=r−i+1s=r-i+1, this interval becomes [μr−s+1+s,λr−s+1+s][\mu_{r-s+1}+s,\lambda_{r-s+1}+s] which is the sths^{\textnormal{th}} set in the transversal presentation of the lattice path matroid 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}. An example is shown in Figure 10. ∎

Rook matroids are shown to be positroids in Section 3.3, and positroids are known to be closed under taking minors [ARW16, Proposition 3.5] and under a cyclic shift of the ground set [ARW16, Lemma 3.3]. Since the map in the proof of Proposition 3.24 is a cyclic shift, we can thus deduce that every lattice path matroid is a positroid, a fact first proven in [Oh11].

3.3. Relation to positroids

Definition 3.25.

Let AA be a full rank d×nd\times n matrix with real entries such that all its maximal minors are non-negative. The representable matroid M⁡(A)M(A) associated to AA is called a positroid.

The property of being a positroid is strongly dependent on the total ordering on the ground set of the matroid; the ordering we use here is the standard ordering for the rook matroid introduced in Section 3. The proof method we use is reminiscent of Oh’s proof of the positroid property of lattice path matroids [Oh11].

Theorem 3.26.

The rook matroid ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} is a positroid.

Proof.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape with rr rows and n−rn-r columns. Define the r×nr\times n matrix F=Ir×r|Dλ/μF=I_{r\times r}|D_{\lambda/\mu} where Ir×rI_{r\times r} is an r×rr\times r identity matrix and Dλ/μD_{\lambda/\mu} is the r×n−rr\times n-r matrix with columns indexed by [r+1,n][r+1,n] and defined by

(Dλ/μ)i,j={(−1)i+r​xij−1if (i,j)∈λ/μ,0otherwise.(D_{\lambda/\mu})_{i,j}=\begin{cases}(-1)^{i+r}x_{i}^{j-1}\quad\text{if $(i,j)\in\lambda/\mu$},\\ 0\qquad\qquad\quad\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

where the xix_{i} for i∈[r]i\in[r] are positive reals whose values we will specify later. Note that the support of FF (i.e. the set of non-zero entries) is exactly the same as that of the incidence matrix corresponding to the set system Aλ/μA_{\lambda/\mu} defined after Fact 3.1. Let B=L⊔JB=L\sqcup J, where L=B∩[r]L=B\cap[r], J=B∩[r+1,n]J=B\cap[r+1,n], and |L|=ℓ|L|=\ell. Let ΔB\Delta_{B} be the minor of FF with columns from BB. By the observation on the support of FF, if BB is not a basis, then ΔB=0\Delta_{B}=0; and if BB is a basis, then ΔB\Delta_{B} has at least one non-zero term in its expansion as a determinant. We show that the term dominating this expansion is positive. Expanding ΔB\Delta_{B} along the columns of LL (each of which is some standard basis vector) from left to right, we pick up a sign equal to (−1)K(-1)^{K}, where K=∑a∈La+ℓ⁡(3−ℓ)2K=\sum_{a\in L}a+\frac{\ell(3-\ell)}{2}. We then extract a factor of (−1)b+r(-1)^{b+r} for each b∈[r]∖Lb\in[r]\setminus L. We are then left with the minor of Dλ/μD_{\lambda/\mu} with rows from [r]∖L[r]\setminus L and columns from JJ. Since BB is a basis, the set JJ can be matched to the rows [r]∖L[r]\setminus L by a non-nesting rook placement. With the rows ordered increasingly and the columns of JJ ordered decreasingly, this matching contributes the anti-diagonal monomial, so the anti-diagonal term of this minor is nonzero. By choosing xix_{i} such that xr>1x_{r}>1 is sufficiently large, and xr−i=xr−i+1r2x_{r-i}=x_{r-i+1}^{r^{2}} for i=1,…,r−1i=1,\ldots,r-1, we see that the anti-diagonal term, i.e., the term arising from the longest permutation on r−ℓr-\ell elements, strictly dominates the sum of the absolute values of all other non-zero terms. This anti-diagonal term has sign (−1)(r−ℓ2)(-1)^{\binom{r-\ell}{2}}. Since the second term in the expression for KK above is equivalent mod 22 to (ℓ+12)\binom{\ell+1}{2}, the gathered powers of −1-1 reduce to

∑a∈La+(ℓ+12)+∑b∈[r]∖L(b+r)+(r−ℓ2)=2​r​(r−ℓ)+ℓ⁡(ℓ+1),\sum_{a\in L}a+\binom{\ell+1}{2}+\sum_{b\in[r]\setminus L}(b+r)+\binom{r-\ell}{2}=2r(r-\ell)+\ell(\ell+1),

which is even and hence the dominant term is positive and ΔB>0\Delta_{B}>0. ∎

Let λ/μ=4433/2\lambda/\mu=4433/2. B=[100000−x16−x170100x24x25x26x270010−x34−x35−x3600001x44x45x460].B=\left[\begin{array}[]{cccc|cccc}1&0&0&0&0&0&-x_{1}^{6}&-x_{1}^{7}\\ 0&1&0&0&x_{2}^{4}&x_{2}^{5}&x_{2}^{6}&x_{2}^{7}\\ 0&0&1&0&-x_{3}^{4}&-x_{3}^{5}&-x_{3}^{6}&0\\ 0&0&0&1&x_{4}^{4}&x_{4}^{5}&x_{4}^{6}&0\end{array}\right].

3.4. Tutte polynomials

In this subsection, we show that the Tutte polynomials of rook matroids and lattice path matroids coincide, thereby tightening the correspondence between these classes of matroids.

The Tutte polynomial is defined as the corank-nullity generating function of the matroid MM:

TM​(x,y)≔∑A⊆E(x−1)r⁡(E)−r⁡(A)​(y−1)|A|−r⁡(A).{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}T_{M}(x,y)}\coloneqq\sum_{A\subseteq E}(x-1)^{r(E)-r(A)}(y-1)^{|A|-r(A)}.

For an overview of results on Tutte polynomials, see [EMM22]. The important fact about the Tutte polynomial that we will use is that it satisfies the deletion-contraction recursion:

(1) TM​(x,y)=TM/e​(x,y)+TM∖e​(x,y),T_{M}(x,y)=T_{M/e}(x,y)+T_{M\setminus e}(x,y),

where e∈Ee\in E is neither a loop nor a coloop.

We need the following lemma, the proof of which is simple and hence omitted.

Lemma 3.28.

Let MM be a rook matroid on a skew shape with rr rows. Then the two deletions M∖rM\setminus r and M∖(r+1)M\setminus(r+1) are isomorphic, and thus have the same Tutte polynomial.

For the purpose of readability, we use T⁡(M,x,y)T(M;x,y) in place of TM​(x,y)T_{M}(x,y) ahead.

Theorem 3.29.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape. Then T⁡(𝒫λ/μ,x,y)=T⁡(ℛλ/μ,x,y)T(\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu};x,y)=T(\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu};x,y).
