In D′D^{\prime} we have removed the first column of DD, in D′′D^{\prime\prime} we have removed the last row of DD, indexed by rr. The last picture indicates that the last row contains a rook.

The Tutte polynomial for the lattice path matroid satisfies

(2) T⁡(𝒫D,x,y)=T⁡(𝒫D′,x,y)+T⁡(𝒫D′′,x,y),T(\mathcal{P}_{D};x,y)=T(\mathcal{P}_{D^{\prime}};x,y)+T(\mathcal{P}_{D^{\prime\prime}};x,y),

by deletion-contraction, which corresponds to conditioning on whether or not the first step in the path is an East step or a North step.

Similarly, the Tutte polynomial for the rook matroid satisfies

(3) T⁡(ℛD,x,y)=T⁡(ℛD∖r,x,y)+T⁡(ℛD′′,x,y),T(\mathcal{R}_{D};x,y)=T(\mathcal{R}_{D}\setminus r;x,y)+T(\mathcal{R}_{D^{\prime\prime}};x,y),

by considering deletion-contraction of the last row index. By Lemma 3.28, we know that T⁡(ℛD∖r,x,y)=T⁡(ℛD∖(r+1),x,y)T(\mathcal{R}_{D}\setminus r;x,y)=T(\mathcal{R}_{D}\setminus(r+1);x,y) = T⁡(ℛD′,x,y)T(\mathcal{R}_{D^{\prime}};x,y). By the induction hypothesis, we have that

T⁡(𝒫D′′,x,y)=T⁡(ℛD′′,x,y)​ and ​T​(𝒫D′,x,y)=T⁡(ℛD′,x,y).T(\mathcal{P}_{D^{\prime\prime}};x,y)=T(\mathcal{R}_{D^{\prime\prime}};x,y)\text{ and }T(\mathcal{P}_{D^{\prime}};x,y)=T(\mathcal{R}_{D^{\prime}};x,y).

Substituting the terms in the RHS of (3) with the expressions above and using (2), it follows that T⁡(𝒫D,x,y)=T⁡(ℛD,x,y)T(\mathcal{P}_{D};x,y)=T(\mathcal{R}_{D};x,y). ∎

The Tutte polynomial is a valuative invariant of a matroid: it behaves well under subdivisions of matroid polytopes. On the basis of Theorem 3.29 and computer experiments, we make the case that every valuative invariant has the same value on ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} as it does on 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}.

Conjecture 3.30.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape and let ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} and 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} be the corresponding rook matroid and lattice path matroid respectively. Then for every valuative invariant ff for matroids, we have

f⁡(ℛλ/μ)=f⁡(𝒫λ/μ).f(\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu})=f(\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}).

In particular, the same would hold for a universal valuative invariant like the Derksen–Fink 𝒢\mathcal{G}-invariant [DF10]. For a systematic treatment of valuative invariants of matroids from a computational viewpoint, see [FS24]. Since our preprint first appeared, Conjecture 3.30 has been proved by Bonin and de Mier in [BdM26] using the concept of the configuration of a matroid.

4. Distributional properties of non-nesting rook numbers

In this section, we use the underlying matroid structure to deduce the distributional properties of the coefficients of the non-nesting rook polynomial. The main result of the following subsection can be seen as a non-nesting analog of the bipartite case of the Heilmann–Lieb theorem on the real-rootedness of the matching polynomial [HL72, Nij76]. For the definition of Lorentzian polynomials, see [BH20].

4.1. Ultra-log-concavity of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu}

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape with rr rows and cc columns. The basis-generating polynomial rλ/μr_{\lambda/\mu} of ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} serves as the appropriate multivariate generalization of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu}, the univariate non-nesting rook polynomial introduced in Section 2.1. To emphasize the role played by column and row variables separately — which will also be useful in Section 5 — we use 𝐱=(x1,…,xr)\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}) and 𝐲=(yr+1,…,yr+c)\mathbf{y}=(y_{r+1},\ldots,y_{r+c}) for the row and column variables of rλ/μr_{\lambda/\mu} respectively. By Theorem 3.3, bases of rook matroids correspond to occupied column indices taken together with unoccupied row indices of rook placements; we can thus write

(4) rλ/μ​(𝐱,𝐲)=∑ρ∈NNλ/μ∏i∈R⁡(ρ)xi​∏j∈C⁡(ρ)yj,r_{\lambda/\mu}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\sum_{\rho\in\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu}}\prod_{i\in R(\rho)}x_{i}\prod_{j\in C(\rho)}y_{j},

where as before NNλ/μ\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu} denotes the set of non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu and R⁡(ρ),C⁡(ρ)R(\rho),C(\rho) correspond to the set of row indices not occupied by ρ\rho and the set of column indices that are occupied by ρ\rho respectively.

Corollary 4.1.

For every skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu, the coefficient sequence of the non-nesting rook polynomial Mλ/μ​(t)=∑k=0rak​(λ/μ)​tkM_{\lambda/\mu}(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{r}a_{k}(\lambda/\mu)t^{k} is ultra-log-concave with no internal zeros. That is,

(ak(rk))2≥ak−1(rk−1)⋅ak+1(rk+1)for all 1≤k≤r−1.\left(\dfrac{a_{k}}{\binom{r}{k}}\right)^{2}\geq\dfrac{a_{k-1}}{\binom{r}{k-1}}\cdot\dfrac{a_{k+1}}{\binom{r}{k+1}}\quad\text{for all $1\leq k\leq r-1$}.

Moreover, there exists a skew shape α/β\alpha/\beta such that Mα/β​(t)M_{\alpha/\beta}(t) is not real-rooted.

Proof.

Suppose λ/μ\lambda/\mu has rr rows and cc columns. Let MM be the rook matroid ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}, PMP_{M} be the corresponding basis-generating polynomial, and T=[r+1,r+c]T=[r+1,r+c]. Consider f⁡(t,s)=PM​(t⋅𝟏T+s⋅𝟏Tc)f(t,s)=P_{M}(t\cdot\mathbf{1}_{T}+s\cdot\mathbf{1}_{T^{c}}) where 𝟏T\mathbf{1}_{T} is the characteristic vector of TT. Note that PMP_{M} can be expressed as in (4). The result then follows from the fact that PMP_{M} is Lorentzian [BH20, Theorem 3.10], specializing variables preserves the Lorentzian property, and a homogeneous bivariate polynomial is Lorentzian if and only if its coefficient sequence is ultra-log-concave with no internal zeros.

The smallest counterexample to the real-rootedness of the non-nesting rook polynomial is given in Corollary 5.10, along with fuller context. ∎

Remark 4.2.

Combining the corollary above with Proposition 3.11, it follows that the generating polynomial of the number of valleys ranging over the set of lattice paths contained inside a partition λ\lambda is ultra-log-concave. Showing this using the matroidal structure of lattice path matroids alone appears to be difficult.

At this juncture, we note the parallel between the non-nesting rook polynomial and the full rook polynomial: both are ultra-log-concave. We will see that this is essentially the strongest property we can hope for, as it turns out that unlike the full rook polynomial the non-nesting counterpart is not real-rooted. In Section 5.2, the proper context of this failure of real-rootedness will be given.

4.2. Lattice path matroids are not HPP

In the previous subsection, we saw that ultra-log-concavity holds for the non-nesting rook numbers. In this subsection, we consider a strengthening of real-rootedness (stability) and give the first explicit example of a lattice path matroid that does not have the half-plane property. For the definitions and overview of stable polynomials in the context of matroid theory, see [Brä15].

A robust necessary condition that a homogeneous, multiaffine polynomial is stable is that its support forms the collection of bases of a matroid [COSW04]. The half-plane property (HPP) of a matroid MM identifies whether the converse is true, namely that the basis-generating polynomial of M=(E,ℬ)M=(E,\mathcal{B}) defined as

PM​(𝐱)=∑B∈ℬ∏i∈Bxi,P_{M}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}}\prod_{i\in B}x_{i},

is stable. We call such a matroid HPP. In [COSW04], an in-depth investigation of the half-plane property for matroids was carried out. One question raised – a “wild speculation” according to [COSW04] – was whether transversal matroids have the HPP. Shortly thereafter, Choe and Wagner provided an example of a rank 44 transversal matroid on 1212 elements that was not HPP [CW06]. Their example, however, is not a lattice path matroid; this can be straightforwardly checked using a criterion described in [BdM06, Theorem 3.14]. To our knowledge, the question of whether lattice path matroids have the HPP is thus still open. The purpose of this subsection is to give the first explicit example of a lattice path matroid—in fact a Catalan matroid—that does not have the half-plane property.

Theorem 4.3.

There exists a generalized Catalan matroid that is not HPP. Concretely, the basis-generating polynomial of the matroid 𝒫λ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda} for λ=666333\lambda=666333 is not stable.

Proof.

Let λ=666333\lambda=666333 and P⁡(𝐱)P(\mathbf{x}) be the basis-generating polynomial of 𝒫λ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}. Consider the univariate polynomial f⁡(t)f(t) obtained by the substitution xi=tx_{i}=t for i=1,…,6i=1,\ldots,6 and xj=1x_{j}=1, for j=7,…,12j=7,\ldots,12 in P⁡(𝐱)P(\mathbf{x}). Using SageMath [The26], we found that

f⁡(t)=t6+36​t5+225​t4+400​t3.f(t)=t^{6}+36t^{5}+225t^{4}+400t^{3}.

This polynomial has non-real roots near −3.6855±0.6232​i.-3.6855\pm 0.6232i. Since specializing variables in stable polynomials to real values preserves stability, it follows that P⁡(𝐱)P(\mathbf{x}) is not stable. ∎

Corollary 4.4.

The Catalan matroid M10M_{10} is not HPP. That is, the basis-generating polynomial of M10M_{10} is not stable.

Proof.

Every generalized Catalan matroid is a minor of some Catalan matroid [BdM06, Theorem 4.2]. In particular, if M10M_{10} denotes the Catalan matroid of order 1010 (defined as the lattice path matroid on the Ferrers shape δ10\delta_{10}), then 𝒫666333\mathcal{P}_{666333} is a minor of M10M_{10}. Since having the half-plane property is closed under taking minors [COSW04], it follows that M10M_{10} cannot have the half-plane property. ∎

Remark 4.5.

In [Xu15] it is stated that the class of generalized Catalan matroids is not HPP, however, no explicit counterexample is given.

5. Rook placements as linear extensions

In this section, we show a bijective correspondence between labeled skew shapes and posets of width two. We obtain an interpretation for the non-nesting rook polynomial in terms of a PP-Eulerian polynomial of a poset and deduce the following results. The PP-Eulerian polynomial of a naturally labeled width two poset is ultra-log-concave, thereby completing the picture of the Neggers–Stanley conjecture, which was disproved using a naturally labeled width two counterexample [Ste07]. We deduce this from a stronger statement, namely that a suitable multivariate analog of the PP-Eulerian polynomial—analogous to the one considered in [BL16]—is Lorentzian. Returning to the rook polynomial setting, we learn that there exists a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu for which the non-nesting rook polynomial Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} has non-real roots. We end by considering the gamma-positivity properties of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu}.

5.1. Neggers–Stanley conjecture

In this subsection we recall the statement and context of the Neggers–Stanley conjecture. For undefined terminology concerning posets, we refer to [Sta11].

Recall that given a poset PP, the width of PP is the size of the largest antichain in PP. A labeling of a poset PP on nn elements is a bijection ω:P→[n]\omega:P\to[n]. We say that ω\omega is a natural labeling if i≺ji\prec j implies ω⁡(i)<ω⁡(j).\omega(i)<\omega(j). The Jordan-Hölder set of (P,ω)(P,\omega) is the set of all permutations of [n][n] the inverses of which are linear extensions of (P,ω)(P,\omega) i.e., it is defined as

ℒ⁡(P,ω)={σ∈𝔖n:i≺j⟹σ−1​(ω⁡(i))<σ−1​(ω⁡(j))}.\mathcal{L}(P,\omega)=\{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}:i\prec j\implies\sigma^{-1}({\omega(i)})<\sigma^{-1}({\omega(j)})\}.

In other words, σ∈ℒ⁡(P)\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P) if for every relation i≺ji\prec j in PP, we have that ω⁡(i)\omega(i) precedes ω⁡(j)\omega(j) in the one-line representation of the permutation σ.\sigma.

The (P,ω)(P,\omega)-Eulerian polynomial, also known as the WW-polynomial of PP, is the descent-generating polynomial of the Jordan-Hölder set of (P,ω)(P,\omega):

WP,ω​(t)=∑σ∈ℒ⁡(P,ω)tdes⁡(σ).W_{P,\omega}(t)=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P,\omega)}t^{\des(\sigma)}.

When ω\omega is natural, we simply write WPW_{P}, since the polynomial is independent of the choice of natural labeling. Observe that in the definitions of the multivariate analog that follow, there is a dependence on the choice of natural labeling that we make explicit.

The distributional properties of WP,ωW_{P,\omega} were of early interest to combinatorialists working in poset theory. The following conjecture was first formulated by Neggers in 1978 for natural labelings ω\omega; in 1986, Stanley extended it to arbitrary labelings. Subsequent references to this conjecture also called it the Poset conjecture [Bre89]. For further background, the reader can consult [Brä15, Section 6].

Conjecture 5.1 (Neggers–Stanley conjecture [Neg78, Sta89]).

Let (P,ω)(P,\omega) be a labeled poset. Then WP,ωW_{P,\omega} is real-rooted.

The Neggers–Stanley conjecture was of central importance to algebraic combinatorics until its resolution in the negative in the early aughts: first by Brändén [Brä04] who found a family of counterexamples to Stanley’s formulation and then Stembridge [Ste07] who disproved Neggers’ counterpart as well. In both cases, the counterexample furnished was of a width two poset; Brändén’s construction was non-naturally labeled while Stembridge’s (larger) counterexample was naturally labeled. Despite this breakthrough, the question of unimodality or log-concavity of WP,ωW_{P,\omega} for general (P,ω)(P,\omega) remained open. In particular, the following conjecture of Brenti has been open since 1989.

Conjecture 5.2.

[Bre89, Conjecture 1.1] Let (P,ω)(P,\omega) be a labeled poset. Then WP,ωW_{P,\omega} is log-concave with no internal zeros.

There have been two positive results towards this end. Reiner and Welker proved that when PP is naturally labeled and graded, WPW_{P} is unimodal and symmetric [RW05]. Brändén then gave an elegant combinatorial proof of a stronger property: namely that WPW_{P} is γ\gamma-positive for the larger class of sign-graded posets [Brä06, Brä08].

In the next subsection, we show a strengthening of Conjecture 5.2 for special posets PP. Namely, we show that when PP is naturally labeled and of width two, then WPW_{P} is ultra-log-concave. We do so by formulating an appropriate multivariate analog of WPW_{P} and recognizing it as the basis-generating polynomial of a rook matroid.

5.2. Matroidal lifts of PP-Eulerian polynomials

Given a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu, our goal is to obtain a suitable poset PP such that the WW-polynomial of PP is equal to the non-nesting rook polynomial of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. We do so in Theorem 5.4. Before we state this, we introduce a multivariate analog of WPW_{P}. Our choice is distinct from, but inspired by, the definition in [BL16].

Let (P,ω)(P,\omega) be a naturally labeled poset of width two. Fix a chain decomposition C1⊔C2C_{1}\sqcup C_{2} of PP where the chain C1C_{1} has rr elements and the chain C2C_{2} has cc elements. We emphasize that the multivariate polynomial W~P,ω\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega} defined ahead depends on the choice of chain decomposition of PP, but the univariate polynomial WP,ωW_{P,\omega} does not. (The chain decomposition of (P,ω)(P,\omega) is unique when PP is irreducible [Ste07, Proposition 5.1].) With respect to this chain decomposition, define W~P,ω∈ℕ[xe,ye′:e∈C1,e′∈C2]\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega}\in\mathbb{N}[x_{e},y_{e^{\prime}}:e\in C_{1},e^{\prime}\in C_{2}] as

(5) W~P,ω​(𝐱,𝐲)=∑σ∈ℒ⁡(P,ω)∏i∈RA​(σ)xi​∏j∈DT​(σ)yj,\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P,\omega)}\prod_{i\in\text{RA}(\sigma)}x_{i}\prod_{j\in\text{DT}(\sigma)}y_{j},

where

  1. (1)

    RA(σ)={σi∈[r+c]:σi>σi−1,σi∈C1}\text{RA}(\sigma)=\{\sigma_{i}\in[r+c]:\sigma_{i}>\sigma_{i-1},\sigma_{i}\in C_{1}\} is the set of row ascents of σ\sigma, i.e. the set of ascent tops lying in C1C_{1} and σ0=−∞\sigma_{0}=-\infty.

  2. (2)

    DT​(σ)={σi∈[r+c]:σi>σi+1}\text{DT}(\sigma)=\{\sigma_{i}\in[r+c]:\sigma_{i}>\sigma_{i+1}\} is the set of descent tops.

The condition in the definition of RA​(σ)\text{RA}(\sigma) implies that the element σ1\sigma_{1} is an ascent top if and only if σ1∈C1\sigma_{1}\in C_{1}, which by virtue of C1C_{1} being a chain with minimum element 11, is equivalent to σ1=1\sigma_{1}=1. Here RA\mathrm{RA} stands for row ascent, for a reason that will be made clear during the course of the proof of Theorem 5.4. Also note that W~P,ω\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega} is homogeneous of degree |C1||C_{1}|. It is not necessarily true that for every natural labeling ω\omega, this polynomial has only 0/10/1 coefficients; this holds, however, in the example below.

Example 5.3.

Recall that if rλ/μr_{\lambda/\mu} is the basis-generating polynomial of the rook matroid on λ/μ\lambda/\mu, then we can express it in terms of row variables x1,…,xrx_{1},\ldots,x_{r} and column variables yr+1,…,yr+cy_{r+1},\ldots,y_{r+c} as

rλ/μ​(𝐱,𝐲)=∑ρ∈NNλ/μ∏i∈R⁡(ρ)xi​∏j∈C⁡(ρ)yj.r_{\lambda/\mu}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\sum_{\rho\in\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu}}\prod_{i\in R(\rho)}x_{i}\prod_{j\in C(\rho)}y_{j}.

We can now state the main theorem of the section.

Theorem 5.4.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape and rλ/μr_{\lambda/\mu} be the basis-generating polynomial of the rook matroid on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. There exists a naturally labeled poset (P,ω)(P,\omega) of width two such that

(6) rλ/μ​(𝐱,𝐲)≅W~P,ω​(𝐱,𝐲)r_{\lambda/\mu}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\cong\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})

where ≅\cong denotes equality up to reindexing of the variables.

Remark 5.5.

The fact that linear extensions of posets of width kk bijectively correspond to lattice paths contained within a compact region of ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k} follows from the standard theory of distributive lattices (see [Dil50] or [Sta11, pg. 296], for example). Similar bijections to ours appear in [CPP22, Lemma 8.1] and an unpublished paper of Stanley [Sta]. The theorem above can be seen as a matroidal and multivariate refinement of the aforementioned results.

Proof of Theorem 5.4.

We begin by relabeling the rows and columns of λ/μ\lambda/\mu in the following manner. Denote the innermost lattice path of the skew shape by Lλ/μL_{\lambda/\mu} and number the rows of λ/μ\lambda/\mu from bottom to top and the columns from left to right by the North and East steps of Lλ/μL_{\lambda/\mu} respectively. Every reference to a cell (i,j)(i,j) of the skew shape is with respect to this labeling. See Figure 11(a) for an example. Let C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} be the two chains defining PP, labeled respectively by the row and column labels of λ/μ\lambda/\mu that were induced by Lλ/μL_{\lambda/\mu}. Let this labeling be ω\omega. Hereafter, in the context of cover relations, we will use i,ji,j in place of ω⁡(i),ω⁡(j)\omega(i),\omega(j).

Add the cover relation i≺⋅ji\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}j to PP for every outer corner (i,j)(i,j) of λ/μ\lambda/\mu and similarly the cover relation j≺⋅ij\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}i for every inner corner (i,j)(i,j). This construction is illustrated in Figure 11(b). We make the following claim:

Claim 1: The poset (P,ω)(P,\omega) is naturally labeled and of width two.

Proof of claim 1: The width two observation is immediate from the construction of PP. To see that PP is naturally labeled, we make an intermediate claim: for every cell (i,j)∈λ/μ(i,j)\in\lambda/\mu (with the above labeling), i<j.i<j. Since the row labels decrease from top to bottom, it suffices to show this for a cell (i,j)(i,j) that is the topmost box in its column. This holds since every topmost box in a column lies directly under or to the right of a 𝙽𝙴\mathtt{NE} segment of the innermost path Lλ/μL_{\lambda/\mu}.

Now consider the cover relation a≺⋅ba\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}b where a∈C1,b∈C2a\in C_{1},b\in C_{2}. This implies that (a,b)(a,b) is an outer corner of the shape. The cell to the immediate left of (a,b)(a,b), say (a,c)(a,c), must lie in λ/μ\lambda/\mu and hence a<ca<c, by the intermediate claim. Since the column labeling increases from left to right, we must also have a<ba<b. The inner corner case is similarly proved, which finishes the proof of the claim.

Now we exhibit a bijection from non-nesting rook placements inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu to elements of the Jordan-Hölder set ℒ⁡(P,ω)\mathcal{L}(P,\omega). This bijection will send non-nesting rook configurations with kk occupied rows to inverses of linear extensions with kk descents. Formally, define f:NNλ/μ→ℒ⁡(P,ω)f:\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu}\to\mathcal{L}(P,\omega) by f=ψ∘Tλ/μf=\psi\circ T_{\lambda/\mu} where Tλ/μ:NNλ/μ→𝒫λ/μT_{\lambda/\mu}:\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu}\to\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} is the bijection between rook placements and lattice paths described in Proposition 3.11 and ψ:𝒫λ/μ→ℒ⁡(P,ω)\psi:\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}\to\mathcal{L}(P,\omega) is the path-to-permutation map ψ⁡(L)=σ=σ1​…​σr+c\psi(L)=\sigma=\sigma_{1}\ldots\sigma_{r+c}, constructed in Definition 3.14. An illustration of this is in Figure 11(c).

Claim 2: The map ff defined above is a bijection.

Proof of Claim 2: By the uniqueness of the permutation representation of the lattice path and the rook-to-path bijection from Proposition 3.11, the map ff is well-defined. To show that ff is a bijection, it suffices to show that ψ\psi is a bijection.

To that end, we first need to show that σ=ψ⁡(L)\sigma=\psi(L) does indeed lie in ℒ⁡(P,ω)\mathcal{L}(P,\omega), whenever LL is a lattice path contained inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Suppose i≺⋅ji\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}j in PP. Two cases arise:

Case 1: Both i,ji,j lie in the same chain of PP, and are hence either both row indices or both column indices; since row indices increase from top to bottom and column indices increase from left to right in the labeling of λ/μ\lambda/\mu, the path LL must traverse step σ−1​(i)\sigma^{-1}(i) before step σ−1​(j)\sigma^{-1}(j) and hence ii must precede jj in σ\sigma.

Case 2: The elements i,ji,j lie in different chains. Without loss of generality, assume that ii is a row index and jj is a column index, so that (i,j)(i,j) is an outer corner of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Then the (σ−1​(i))th(\sigma^{-1}(i))^{\textnormal{th}} and (σ−1​(j))th(\sigma^{-1}(j))^{\textnormal{th}} steps of LL are respectively North and East steps. Let QQ be the lower boundary path of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Since (i,j)(i,j) is an outer corner, QQ has a North-East segment at this corner. Let (ψ⁡(Q))k=i(\psi(Q))_{k}=i, so that (ψ⁡(Q))k+1=j(\psi(Q))_{k+1}=j. Since LL is contained in λ/μ\lambda/\mu, it lies weakly above QQ. Hence the North step of LL in row ii occurs no later than the corresponding North step of QQ, while the East step of LL in column jj occurs no earlier than the corresponding East step of QQ. This implies that σ\sigma satisfies σ−1​(i)≤k<k+1≤σ−1​(j)\sigma^{-1}(i)\leq k<k+1\leq\sigma^{-1}(j), as required. The case where i,ji,j are respectively column and row indices is analogous, using the upper boundary path of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. This shows that the image of ff lies in ℒ⁡(P,ω).\mathcal{L}(P,\omega).

To see that ψ\psi is a surjection, consider σ∈ℒ⁡(P,ω)\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P,\omega). Define a lattice path LL by letting the ithi^{\textnormal{th}} step of LL be North if σi\sigma_{i} is in C1C_{1} and East if σi\sigma_{i} is in C2C_{2}; such a path certainly satisfies ψ⁡(L)=σ\psi(L)=\sigma once we verify that LL is contained inside the shape. To do so, suppose LL exits the skew shape via the lower boundary of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Then there exists an outer corner (i,j)(i,j) of λ/μ\lambda/\mu such that j​iji forms an 𝙴𝙽\mathtt{EN} step of LL. In particular σ=σ1​…​j​i​…​σr+c\sigma=\sigma_{1}\ldots ji\ldots\sigma_{r+c}. Now (i,j)(i,j) is an outer corner which implies that i≺⋅ji\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}j and since σ∈ℒ⁡(P,ω)\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P,\omega), ii must precede jj in σ\sigma, a contradiction. The case where LL exits through the upper boundary is analogous: one obtains an inner corner (i,j)(i,j) such that i​jij forms an 𝙽𝙴\mathtt{NE} segment of LL, contradicting the relation j≺⋅ij\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}i. Thus LL is a lattice path contained within λ/μ\lambda/\mu and hence ψ\psi is a surjection, and ff is indeed a bijection.

Claim 3: Let ρ\rho be the rook placement that corresponds to σ\sigma under the bijection ff. Then

C⁡(ρ)=DT​(σ)andR⁡(ρ)=RA​(σ).C(\rho)=\text{DT}(\sigma)\quad\text{and}\quad R(\rho)=\text{RA}(\sigma).

That is, under the innermost path labeling of λ/μ\lambda/\mu, occupied columns of ρ\rho and the unoccupied rows of ρ\rho are precisely equal to the descent tops of σ\sigma and row ascents of σ\sigma respectively.

Proof of Claim 3: Let Tλ/μ​(ρ)T_{\lambda/\mu}(\rho) be the lattice path Lρ=LL_{\rho}=L and let σL\sigma_{L} be the path permutation of LL, with the convention that σ0=−∞\sigma_{0}=-\infty. Then

C⁡(ρ)=ψ⁡({East steps of inner valleys of L})={σiL∈C2:σiL>σi+1L}=DT​(σ),andC(\rho)=\psi(\{\text{East steps of inner valleys of $L$}\})\\ =\{\sigma^{L}_{i}\in C_{2}:\sigma^{L}_{i}>\sigma^{L}_{i+1}\}\\ =\text{DT}(\sigma),\quad\text{and}
R⁡(ρ)=C1∖ψ⁡({North steps of inner valleys of L})={σiL∈C1:σi−1L<σiL}=RA​(σ).R(\rho)=C_{1}\setminus\psi(\{\text{North steps of inner valleys of $L$}\})=\{\sigma^{L}_{i}\in C_{1}:\sigma^{L}_{i-1}<\sigma^{L}_{i}\}=\text{RA}(\sigma).

This completes the proof of the assertion that W~P,ω\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega} can be written as a multivariate generating polynomial of non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. To finish, we note that after reindexing the rows and columns of the skew shape in accordance with the matroid labeling, this latter polynomial is precisely the basis-generating polynomial of ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}. ∎

Let ℰ\mathcal{E} be the map from Theorem 5.4 that takes a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu to a width two poset PP. From the construction in the proof above, it is implicit that ℰ\mathcal{E} is injective. We record the surjectivity of ℰ\mathcal{E} in the lemma below.

Lemma 5.6.

For every poset PP of width two, there exists a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu such that ℰ⁡(λ/μ)=P\mathcal{E}(\lambda/\mu)=P.

Proof.

First we repeatedly delete unique minimal and unique maximal elements of PP, whenever they exist, until no such element remains. (This reduction is harmless since the skew shape corresponding to the non-reduced poset is obtained from that of the reduced one by prepending empty rows and empty columns.) Once the poset — which by a minor abuse of notation we continue to denote by PP — has two minimal and two maximal elements, proceed as follows.

Let {t1,…,tr+c}\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{r+c}\} be the elements of PP and let C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} be the two chains of PP of length rr and cc respectively. Define λ/μ\lambda/\mu to be the skew shape with rr rows (labeled from bottom to top by elements of C1C_{1}) and cc columns (labeled from left to right by elements of C2C_{2}) such that:

  1. (1)

    There is an inner corner at (ti,tj)(t_{i},t_{j}) for every cover relation of the form ti≺⋅tjt_{i}\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}t_{j} where ti∈C2t_{i}\in C_{2} and tj∈C1t_{j}\in C_{1}.

  2. (2)

    There is an outer corner at (ti,tj)(t_{i},t_{j}) for every cover relation of the form ti≺⋅tjt_{i}\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}t_{j} where ti∈C1t_{i}\in C_{1} and tj∈C2t_{j}\in C_{2}.

By the correspondence between corners and cover relations detailed in the proof of Theorem 5.4, this is precisely the skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu such that ℰ⁡(λ/μ)=P\mathcal{E}(\lambda/\mu)=P. ∎

Remark 5.7.

Let (P,ω′)(P,\omega^{\prime}) be a naturally labeled poset. While Theorem 5.4 and Lemma 5.6 together yield a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu such that (ℰ⁡(λ/μ),ω)(\mathcal{E}(\lambda/\mu),\omega) is a naturally labeled poset satisfying ℰ⁡(λ/μ)=P\mathcal{E}(\lambda/\mu)=P, the two natural labelings ω,ω′\omega,\omega^{\prime} might differ. This will not matter for us, however, since the polynomial WPW_{P} is independent of the natural labeling.

Theorem 5.4 and Lemma 5.6 together allow one to draw mutually enriching connections between PP-Eulerian polynomials and non-nesting rook polynomials. In what follows, we gather corollaries of this correspondence.

To begin, we note that the ultra-log-concavity consequence of the Neggers–Stanley conjecture is true for naturally labeled width two posets. We can deduce an analogous result for the polynomial EP​(t)=∑j=1|P|ej​(P)​tjE_{P}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{|P|}e_{j}(P)t^{j} where ej​(P)e_{j}(P) denotes the number of surjective order–preserving maps from PP to [j][j]. An alternative formulation of the Neggers–Stanley conjecture for naturally labeled posets PP asserts the real-rootedness of EPE_{P}.

Corollary 5.8.

Let PP be a naturally labeled poset of width two and λ/μ\lambda/\mu be the skew shape obtained from Lemma 5.6. Then the WW-polynomial of PP equals the non-nesting rook polynomial of λ/μ\lambda/\mu:

(7) WP​(t)=Mλ/μ​(t),W_{P}(t)=M_{\lambda/\mu}(t),

and hence WPW_{P} is ultra-log-concave. Consequently, EPE_{P} is also ultra-log-concave.

Proof.

Since every natural labeling of the poset PP gives rise to the same WPW_{P}, assume PP has the canonical labeling ω\omega. By Theorem 5.4, the polynomial W~P,ω\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega} is equal, up to a relabeling of the variables, to the basis-generating polynomial of the rook matroid on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. The latter polynomial is Lorentzian [BH20, Theorem 3.10], and this property is preserved under a linear change of variables [BH20, Theorem 2.10]. The aforementioned relabeling maps 𝐱\mathbf{x} variables (resp. 𝐲\mathbf{y} variables) labeled by elements of C1C_{1} (resp. C2C_{2}) to 𝐱\mathbf{x} variables labeled by rows 1,…,r1,\ldots,r (resp. columns r+1,…,r+cr+1,\ldots,r+c) of the skew shape. Thus, by specializing the 𝐱\mathbf{x} variables to 11 and the 𝐲\mathbf{y} variables to tt in (6), we obtain (7). The ultra-log-concavity statement of WPW_{P} then follows from Corollary 4.1. Finally, the ultra-log-concavity of EPE_{P} follows from [BFJ24, Lemma 2.5 (ii)]. ∎

In particular, the PP-Eulerian polynomial of Stembridge’s counterexample to the Neggers–Stanley conjecture is ultra-log-concave, despite not being real-rooted. Figure 12 shows Stembridge’s counterexample and the associated skew shape; the PP-Eulerian polynomial is computed in Corollary 5.10.

A simple but immediate consequence of this correspondence is that Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} can be interpreted as the h∗h^{*}-polynomial of an order polytope. The context for this is a conjecture on the unimodality of the h∗h^{*}-polynomial of lattice polytopes with the integral decomposition property [SVL13]; see [Bra16] for a survey on unimodality problems in Ehrhart theory.

Corollary 5.9.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape, PP be the corresponding naturally labeled poset obtained from Theorem 5.4, and 𝒪⁡(P)\mathcal{O}(P) be the order polytope of PP. Then

Mλ/μ​(t)=h𝒪⁡(P)∗​(t).M_{\lambda/\mu}(t)=h^{*}_{\mathcal{O}(P)}(t).

In particular, the h∗h^{*}-polynomial of the order polytope of a naturally labeled width two poset is ultra-log-concave.

Proof.

The proof is immediate from Theorem 5.4 together with the well-known fact that for a naturally labeled poset PP, its PP-Eulerian polynomial coincides with the h∗h^{*}-polynomial of its order polytope; see, for example, [BS18, Theorem 6.3.11]. ∎

In the other direction of the poset–skew shape correspondence, one can use known results on PP-Eulerian polynomials to deduce distributional properties of the non-nesting rook numbers, extending the results in Section 4. We mention two such applications below.

Stembridge’s width two counterexample to the Neggers–Stanley conjecture [Ste07] shows that real-rootedness of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} can fail in general. This counterexample is illustrated in Figure 12 together with the corresponding skew shape. The following corollary gives a rook-theoretic and matroid-theoretic context within which Stembridge’s counterexample can be understood.

Corollary 5.10.

The non-nesting rook polynomial Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} is not real-rooted in general. Concretely, Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} is not real-rooted for the skew shape λ/μ=888888765/76654321\lambda/\mu=888888765/76654321.

Proof.

Let λ/μ=888888765/76654321\lambda/\mu=888888765/76654321. Applying Corollary 5.8, we obtain the poset on the left in Figure 12, which we recognize as Stembridge’s counterexample to Neggers’ formulation of the Poset conjecture. Thus Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} is not real-rooted.

Alternatively, using SageMath [The26], one can compute Mλ/μ​(t)M_{\lambda/\mu}(t) to be:

Mλ/μ​(t)=3​t8+86​t7+658​t6+1946​t5+2534​t4+1420​t3+336​t2+32​t+1.M_{\lambda/\mu}(t)=3t^{8}+86t^{7}+658t^{6}+1946t^{5}+2534t^{4}+1420t^{3}+336t^{2}+32t+1.

This polynomial has non-real zeros near −1.85884±0.14976​i-1.85884\pm 0.14976i. ∎

Remark 5.11.

By the experimental evidence gathered in [Ste07] and the poset–skew shape correspondence above, it follows that λ/μ=888888765/76654321\lambda/\mu=888888765/76654321 is the smallest skew shape (by size) for which Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} fails to be real-rooted. It would be interesting to find a large class of skew shapes for which real-rootedness holds.

Using the skew shape – poset correspondence, we can also deduce precisely when the non-nesting rook polynomial is palindromic, i.e. when its coefficient sequence (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n} satisfies ak=an−ka_{k}=a_{n-k}, for k=0,…,nk=0,\ldots,n. A palindromic polynomial A⁡(t)A(t) can always be expressed in the following basis:

A⁡(t)=∑k=0⌊n2⌋γk​tk​(1+t)n−2​kA(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor}\gamma_{k}t^{k}(1+t)^{n-2k}

When the coefficients satisfy γk≥0\gamma_{k}\geq 0 for all kk, A⁡(t)A(t) is called γ\gamma-positive; this property is known to imply unimodality of A⁡(t)A(t).

The skew shapes that satisfy symmetry of the non-nesting rook polynomial are defined below.

Definition 5.12.

A skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a squarecase if the bounding rectangle of λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a square and all inner and outer corners of λ/μ\lambda/\mu are of the form (i,r+i)(i,r+i).

For such shapes, γ\gamma-positivity — and hence unimodality — holds for the non-nesting rook polynomial. This fact is not immediately obvious from the combinatorics of rook placements alone. In the proof below, the direct sum of skew shapes is an operation defined in the proof of Lemma 3.5.

Corollary 5.13.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape. Then Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} is palindromic if and only if λ/μ\lambda/\mu is the direct sum of squarecase skew shapes. When this holds, Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} is γ\gamma-positive.

Proof.

It suffices to show that the result holds for connected skew shapes. This is because for skew shapes D1,D2D_{1},D_{2} the polynomial MD1⊕D2=MD1⋅MD2M_{D_{1}\oplus D_{2}}=M_{D_{1}}\cdot M_{D_{2}} is palindromic if and only if each MDiM_{D_{i}} is palindromic for i=1,2i=1,2.

By the poset – skew shape correspondence and the well-known criterion for the palindromicity of PP-Eulerian polynomials [Sta11, Corollary 3.15.18], Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} is palindromic if and only if the corresponding width two poset is graded. By unwinding what the graded condition means for the skew shape, we find that it holds if and only if the inner and outer corners of λ/μ\lambda/\mu are of the form (i,r+i)(i,r+i), where rr is the number of rows of the skew shape. The γ\gamma-positivity of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} then follows from Theorem 5.4 and [Brä06, Theorem 4.2]. ∎
